 A St. Mary's County landmark is no more after the commissioners decided to terminate the lease of the Leonard Hall Junior Naval Academy Tuesday in Leonardtown.The school's lease was slated to end June 30, but the school closed last week.
"It's not about wanting to cancel somebody's lease," Commissioner Mike Hewitt said. "It's not about wanting to take away a school that has been in this county for over 100 years. It's about trying to find a plan that allows that school to continue."
The situation became sticky last week when a letter about the closing of the school was prematurely sent to the school, which is in the same complex of buildings where the commissioners meet weekly.
"That was our mistake," Commissioner President Randy Guy said.
The school was paying county government $12,000 a year in rent.
The commissioners voted Tuesday to end the lease, but Commissioner Eric Colvin was against closing the school.
"I've heard the incredible impact the school has had in helping students turn their lives around," he said. "My opposition in ending this lease is that I did not feel as if there were enough alternatives evaluated. I felt that we could have worked with the school a little bit more to try and find a solution and I'm still opposed to it."
A handful of supporters of the school, including alumni, attended the meeting, though no one spoke to the commissioners. When asked, the group said Headmistress Sarah Green was not in attendance.
Olivia Flynn, one of the supporters, said on Tuesday the school had positively impacted her.
Her first year at the school she received 52 infractions in one quarter — three are enough to warrant discipline — but that number dwindled rapidly over the next few years and she said graduated as a top student leader in 2018.
"It's a process and its a fellowship with the teachers and a mentorship built with the administrators," Flynn said in an interview with Southern Maryland News after Tuesday's meeting. "It helped me deal with conflict, it also helped me build good relationships with people and helped me prepare for life."
Flynn returned to the school which served grades 6 through 12, in 2022 as a history, English and algebra teacher.
County Attorney Buffy Giddens went over a timeline of events, beginning with the school being given a fresh 10-year lease in 2013.
On Feb. 28, 2023, the county received an email request from Green to renew the lease as well as fix the AC unit, which was estimated to be about $100,000.
In May, an assessment looked at 27 systems, which discovered a host of needed repairs and maintenance. The estimate was $575,000 with the school on the hook for about $250,000.
Flynn said "no one else in the school was informed" of the needed upgrades, despite the school's extensive alumni and parent network.
Three months later, the commissioners advised Green of the maintenance issues identified in the facilities assessment and requested a financial sustainability plan by the end of 2023.
"We wanted to give them a chance to rectify the situation," Hewitt said. "We told them, 'We need to hear from you, we need to hear your plan,' but we didn't hear anything for a couple of months."
Green was unable to be reached for comment this week by Southern Maryland News.
Hewitt said the school retained an attorney in October.
"My first thought was, 'Why are you wasting money on an attorney? We need you to get to work on this,'" he said. "Then commissioners are no longer talking to headmistresses, [instead] attorneys are talking to attorneys."
Green submitted 10-year and 15-year plans on Dec. 22. One of the points in the plan was to apply for a grant, which was dependent on a long-term lease from the county and was due by Jan. 12.
Hewitt said the grant would have provided a maximum of just $100,000, and added most schools receive about $23,000.
"Years ago that was a thriving school with hundreds of kids," Hewitt said of Leonard Hall, which had 38 students this year before it closed. "It's not that way anymore. It wasn't the idea that we wanted to close the school. We don't, but the business plan just isn't working."
Hewitt added that "subsidizing the cost of a private school is not in the best interest of all the citizens. It's not fair to the thousands of people who send their kids to public school that the county subsidize a private school."
Hewitt said the commissioners have even looked at other locations for the school and added, "If something can be worked out in the future, we're more than willing to revisit it."

title: CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones
content:
CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The numbers and members just keep growing.Only four months after 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County held its inaugural meeting, the budding philanthropic group is steadily increasing its membership — and the dollars donated to local nonprofits.
On Monday evening, dozens of group members packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library to hear brief presentations on three nonprofits seeking funding: CarePacks of Talbot County, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center and the St. Michaels Fire Department.
After a lightning round of questions and answers, followed by a quick tally of votes cast for the nonprofit members felt was most deserving, CarePacks was selected to receive $15,000 in funding.
Founded by Emily Moody and Easton Mayor Megan Cook, the program serves a large percentage of Talbot County students who rely on meals provided by the school system Monday through Friday, but who may not have access to consistent nutrition over the weekends.
"Kids who are worried about such a basic need as having enough to eat, they simply can't learn," Moody said. "The anxiety of food insecurity is real — it shows up in visits to the nurse for headaches and stomachaches. It shows up on test scores and in classroom behaviors. And sometimes, students will just tell you."
CarePacks serves to comfort the fear and anxiety of food insecurity, she said, and that's done by discreetly placing a bag of meals, snacks and fruit in a student's backpack every week.
Though CarePacks was the clear winner in the number of votes, a desire to help ChesMRC and the St. Michaels Fire Department was evident.
"Are we allowed to vote for two?" one member called out.
While each woman can only cast one vote for the nonprofit of their choice, members can still independently donate to other nonprofits, said Amanda David, one of the group's founding members.
At the group's inaugural meeting in September, one nonprofit that presented but was not selected to receive funding did report an influx in donations the next morning, she added.
Just through bringing local nonprofits in front of a large group of women ready to donate, 100+ Women Who Care raises awareness to funding needs in organizations some community members may not even know about.
"This is a win-win-win situation," David said.
Monday's award was a $2,000 increase from the $13,000 donated to Talbot Interfaith Shelter in September, further marking the group's progression in creating a simple way to engage in local philanthropic efforts.
To Karen Gadson, one of the group's founding members, the concept has "caught fire" primarily due to it being an easy concept.
The group meets for one hour, three times a year. Each woman commits to donating $300 a year — $100 per meeting — to local nonprofits. Members unable to attend in person can cast absentee ballots ahead of time, with group leaders sharing more information about the selected nonprofit afterwards.
"I think it's just been the power of word of mouth," David said of the increase in membership. "I think a lot of women are really impressed with the ease of it, the simplicity behind it, and they've been telling their friends."
And with an already-promising increase from the first meeting, group leaders are working to continue building momentum in Talbot County.
The group is prioritizing weekly communications with members, engaging with local nonprofits and manning a booth at the St. Michaels Farmers Market, David said.
Its social media presence is expanding, too — the group can also be found on Facebook by searching "Women Who Care Talbot County."
David said she was "blown away" by the positive response from women in the community, and her hopes are set high for growing both membership numbers and funding.
"I'd love to fill the Avalon, that would be my goal — our goal is to fill the Avalon and get as many women involved as possible," she said.
The group's next meeting is Monday, May 13, from 5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. at the Talbot County Free Library in Easton.
Members will be considering a new set of nonprofits, including the Mid-Shore Early Learning Center, Tilghman Area Youth Association and For All Seasons.
For more information and to join, visit 100womentalbot.org.

title: Teacher, Support Staff of the Year nominations now open
author: TALBOT COUNTY PUBLIC SCHOOLS
content:
Teacher, Support Staff of the Year nominations now open

 February 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TALBOT COUNTY PUBLIC SCHOOLS | Section: Life 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Public Schools has begun the process to select the 2024-2025 Teacher of the Year and Support Staff of the Year.Any member of the community may nominate a candidate to apply to be Talbot's Teacher of the Year or Support Staff of the Year. The nomination forms are available on the TCPS website at tcps.k12.md.us/2024-teacher-and-support-staff-of-the-year/.
The deadline for nominations for both Teacher of the Year and Support Staff of the Year is Friday, Feb. 9.
A teacher must meet the following requirements to be considered for the Talbot County Teacher of the Year:
Hold state certification in area(s) of assignment, Pre-K through 12th Grade;
Be a current full-time classroom teacher as defined by a teaching contract, to include: librarians, specialists, intervention teachers, ESL teachers, gifted education teachers, instructional coaches and special education teachers;
Have a minimum of six years of exemplary teaching experience (can include this current school year). The last two years must be with Talbot County Public Schools;
Plan to continue in an active teaching status for at least one year; and
Submit a professional resume that addresses the following: Education, Certifications, Experience, Leadership and Awards/Other Recognition.
The purpose of the Support Staff of the Year Award is to recognize an outstanding educational support professional for his/her contribution to the success of the learning community, and to focus public attention on the importance the individuals in these vital roles. To be considered for the Talbot County Support Staff of the Year Award, nominees must meet the following selection Criteria:
Must be full-time employees who have worked for TCPS for a minimum of two years. Any member of the community can nominate a Support Staff Employee.
An exceptionally dedicated, knowledgeable and skilled member of the Support Staff in a school or office;
Goes above and beyond the call of duty;
Is supportive of the learning environment;
Is employed in a non-certified, non-exempt position (A&S staff, exempt employees, teachers and licensed professionals are not eligible.)
The nomination forms for both awards must include a minimum 200-word statement about the nominee's qualifications.
"The Talbot Teacher of the Year and Support Staff of the Year recognition is truly a highlight of the school year," said, Dr. Helga Einhorn Assistant Superintendent for Teaching, Learning & Leading. "This event gives us the opportunity to celebrate some of our most outstanding educators for their innovation, dedication and commitment to our students."

title: Sense of urgency needed on school absenteeism
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Sense of urgency needed on school absenteeism

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 634
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland State Department of Education, Maryland Association of Boards of Education and Public School Superintendents' Association of Maryland met recently with members of the Ways and Means Committee in the Maryland House of Delegates.At that meeting, all three advocacy groups expressed their support for fully funding the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, also known as the Kirwan Report.
Along with the Blueprint for Maryland's Future there is another issue that has had and will have a significant impact on public education in Maryland.
That issue is chronic absenteeism.
The Maryland Department of Education defines chronic absenteeism as missing more than 20 days in a school year, no matter the reason.
WYPR, the public broadcasting corporation's flagship radio station in Baltimore, recently introduced a news report on this issue with the following lead in:
"Chronic absenteeism 'real concern' Maryland lawmakers and educators aim to address."
WYPR cited Maryland Board of Education data indicating that over one-third of Maryland K-12 students missed 10% or more school days last year, with 54.1% of Baltimore City students and 34.7% of Baltimore County students hitting that mark.
The consequences of chronic absenteeism are serious and long lasting.
Maryland Board of Education President Clarence Crawford has observed that "chronic absenteeism can adversely impact a child for a lifetime." He noted research has shown that "chronic absenteeism impacts test scores, grades and children's ability to be able to graduate." He also noted "chronic absenteeism increases the likelihood of engagement with the criminal justice system."
Especially disheartening in the Maryland Board of Education data that nearly 35% of children in kindergarten statewide are chronically absent.
Sue Fothergill, a senior fellow at Attendance Works (a national nonprofit dedicated to raising awareness about the negative impacts of absenteeism), says: "In early grades, some of our families think, 'Well, it's just kindergarten, or it's just first grade, children can miss a few days here and there, it's not that big of a deal.' The reality though, is that those are the most important formative years, not just for learning to read, but learning social emotional skills and establishing habits that help those young people throughout their careers. When a child is chronically absent in kindergarten, they are less likely to be proficient in reading by third grade as at that point, teachers often switch to content-focused learning. It becomes much harder to catch a child up and be able to learn how to read as they matriculate through their years, because they've missed those formative years."
Gov. Wes Moore and state lawmakers are aware of and have already demonstrated a level of concern and action on this problem.
At a recent "Improving Student Achievement" event in Washington, D.C., Moore said, "We know that there are real obstacles we still have to address."
In the Statehouse and the state Senate, legislation has been introduced to establish a task force to study chronic absenteeism in Maryland's public schools.
The legislation as introduced, requires the task force to report its findings and recommendations to the governor and General Assembly by Dec. 1.
Going forward, local and state funding levels for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future will continue to generate enormous amounts of dialogue and deliberation at local governments throughout Maryland and in the General Assembly. That is to be expected as the Blueprint is a multi-year initiative that mandates a projected $3.8 billion increase above current levels of local and state funding for public education in Maryland.
A critical element of success in public education requires more than mandated increases of local and state funding.
It requires more than awareness of, concern about, and discussions on the issue of chronic absenteeism.
What is needed is a sense of urgency on action to address chronic absenteeism in every public school in Maryland.
David Reel is a consultant who provides counsel and services on strategy, advocacy and media on public affairs issues. He lives in Easton.

title: New Fellowship of Christian Athletes club unites and inspires students
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
New Fellowship of Christian Athletes club unites and inspires students

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Life 
 
 712
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — As inspirational music plays, students filled the classroom."Get in here and eat donuts! What are you doing buddy? What's up pal?" Jeff Simmons welcomes everyone with his energetic and contagious excitement.
It's 7:30 a.m. on a Tuesday morning. School won't begin for more than an hour. What brings middle schoolers, teachers and community members out early before school?
For some students in Queen Anne and Talbot Counties, it's a new club called Fellowship of Christian Athletes. This club, or huddle, welcomes not only athletes but anyone who wants to come and make a difference.
Although FCA may be new to some local schools, it is well-known around the world. For over 60 years, FCA has had one mission — "unite your two passions, faith and athletics, to impact the world for Jesus Christ."
Founder Don McClanen started FCA after reading that 30 million American youth had no religious training. McClanen began posting his articles in the locker room and praying before games. Soon, he was dreaming of a way for well-known Christian athletes to advertise their faith on television and in magazines the way they advertised other household products. Currently, FCA is in 115 countries with over 20,000 huddle meetings occurring around the world.
At their first huddle, Centreville Middle students spent time together in fellowship.
The "Walk Out Faith'' huddle activity included scripture readings, a memory verse and relevant questions asking teens how they can grow their faith while also building the community around them.
Seventh Grade Social Studies teacher Thomas Hayman helps oversee the FCA huddle with other school staff. A former church youth director and a current Queen Anne's County Public Schools Teacher of the Year finalist, Hayman is dedicated to teaching and investing in his students. His loyalty doesn't go unnoticed, Hayman's students said he's told them he would even "take a bullet" to keep them safe.
Hayman said it was fate that allowed him to meet Simmons, a former CMS tutor, at the school and fate that put him in this position. Hayman said he is looking forward to the fellowship afforded by FCA "to get together, have fun and see what kind of positive change we can make."
Simmons is the area director of the Fellowship of Christian Athletes) for Queen Anne's and Talbot counties.
He said he had not heard of FCA until a friend suggested he look into it. After research and attending some huddle meetings, he said he was "blown away by what they were doing, how they were doing it, and the impact it had.
In his new position, Simmons has to annually raise his entire budget. The success here is directly linked to the local community's involvement, Simmons said.
With all the huddles happening, there were still many middle and high schools in both Queen Anne's and Talbot counties that had no FCA presence and did not have the same opportunities.
In this monthly email update, Simmons wrote, "There are 9 schools (middle and high) between both counties that do not have any sort of FCA on their campuses."
With the generous support of the community, the 2024 FCA budget for Queen Anne's and Talbot counties was fully funded.
"Thanks to God's provision, coming in the form of generous one time donations and support from those who signed on as Monthly Partners, we reached the amount needed to support the program's budget for 2024" Simmons said.
"In order to establish FCA programming in the remaining schools, we need to fully fund our FCA budget with recurring donations," Simmons shared. "Securing our annual budget with recurring monthly support will allow us to start planning for the future of FCA on the Eastern Shore. This will allow us to not only provide resources and support to the huddles that are already up and running, but also to establish a FCA presence in the schools without one currently."
"Your support, whether it be in financial contributions, prayer and encouragement," Simmons continued, "has confirmed this community's commitment to see Jesus glorified and lives changed through this ministry, and I am so grateful that we all get to be a part of it. God is working on the Shore through these coaches, students, and leaders and I know that the best is yet to come!"
If you would like more information or would like to volunteer, email Jeff Simmons at jsimmons@fca.org.

title: Talbot Board of Education passes FY2025 budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Talbot Board of Education passes FY2025 budget

 February 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 301
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The proposed Talbot County Public Schools fiscal year 2025 budget is headed to the County Council for final approval.At a Talbot County Board of Education meeting Wednesday evening, board members voted to approve the budget and send it to the Talbot County Council.
The proposed unrestricted operating budget is $79.9 million dollars. This is a nearly $7.9 million increase from fiscal year 2024.
TCPS Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones said that while this seems like a larger increase than recent years, the increase is meant to offset a decrease in federal funding.
"This unrestricted budget coupled with the decrease in all of our federal programs nets to a 3.4% increase," she said.
This means that the district is asking for a total of 3.4% more money than it received for fiscal year 2024.
TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi said the district is losing $4.8 million in grant funding for fiscal year 2025.
TCPS Director of Communications Debbie Gardner said in an interview that the $4.8 million came from two COVID-19 related grants — the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund and the Maryland Leads grant.
The proposed capital budget for fiscal year 2025 is $12.1 million. title: TCPS gives Blueprint updates
author: Maggie Trovato

TCPS gives Blueprint updates

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Updates regarding the Blueprint for Maryland's Future were shared at a Talbot County Board of Education meeting Wednesday.The Blueprint is a plan, passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021, that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion each year over the next 10 years
Helga Einhorn, Talbot County Public Schools assistant superintendent for curriculum and instruction, gave updates at the meeting.
Einhorn said the Maryland State Department of Education has approved the College and Career Readiness Standard.
The approved standard — which determines whether students are mastering the standards necessary to prepare them for dual enrollment, advanced placement, post-secondary education and careers — offers two options.
First, students can be considered college and career ready if they have earned a high school grade point average of at least 3.0 and either earned an A, B or C in Algebra I or scored proficient or above on the Algebra I Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program.
The second way students can be considered college and career ready is if they score proficient or above on the English Language Arts 10 MCAP and Algebra I MCAP.
Einhorn said that if students do not meet the College and Career Readiness Standard, a team from the school will meet with that student and their family to develop a plan to get them on track.
Einhorn said this new standard will go into effect immediately. However, she said the interim standard will also remain in effect until July 1, 2025.
The interim standard states that students can be considered college and career ready if they achieve certain scores on either the Partnership for Assessment of Readiness for College and Careers, the early fall MCAP or the spring MCAP for both English 10 and either Algebra I, Algebra II or Geometry.
Another update Einhorn gave at the meeting is that the district has hired Sharon Gaskins as a strategic facilitator to support the district's efforts with the Blueprint.
"(Gaskins) has over 25 years in education and really has been a change agent working with organizations to ensure that they meet their goals," Einhorn said.
Einhorn said the district was able hire Gaskins using grant funding through the Blueprint's Accountability and Implementation Board.
Einhorn also gave an update on a report that the district will need to submit to the Accountability and Implementation Board and MSDE by March 15.
The report will detail the district's implementation of the Blueprint so far. Einhorn said this includes discussing any challenges the district might be facing with implementation.
This report is a way for the state to monitor that school districts are "able to transform" through reshaping and adapting new polices and practices that create a more equitable system, Einhorn said.
"I'm here tonight to assure you that we will meet that March 15 deadline," she said. "And I look forward to sharing some of the findings in that report."

title: School board adopts 2024-2025 calendar
author: Connie Connolly
content:
School board adopts 2024-2025 calendar

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 743
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County students will be heading back to school before Labor Day this year.Offered two alternatives — a pre- or post-Labor Day start — the five-member Board of Education voted unanimously Feb. 6 to approve the pre-Labor Day calendar for the 2024-2025 school year.
English, Spanish and Haitian Creole translations of the calendar are posted on the Caroline County Public Schools website.
The school year start date is Wednesday, Aug. 28.
CCPS Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons presented the two calendars, along with results of a survey distributed to parents, teachers and staff.
While the current school year calendar began after Labor Day, the school board considered factors that mitigated against the later start, including the presidential election day, which necessitates closing schools Tuesday, Nov. 5, and Christmas falling on a Wednesday.
Fall sports practices will begin Aug. 14. Winter break will begin Dec. 20.
The calendar committee emailed a link to the survey Jan. 12 to over 5,400 parents, guardians and all CCPS staff members. A reminder email was sent Jan. 22, and the survey was closed Jan. 26. Some community members provided feedback, as well.
Although 75% of the 3,500 parents and guardians who responded favored a post-Labor Day start, 696 staff respondents, or 70% preferred a pre-Labor Day start.
Before reviewing the feedback, Simmons cautioned the school board, saying, "No matter what decision you make, you're going to make people upset, period. There is no perfect calendar, period."
Board member and retired Caroline County teacher Donna DiGiacomo favored the earlier start.
"So, one calendar starts Aug 28; the other starts Sept. 3, but the end date is just one day difference," DiGiacomo said. The adopted calendar gets "students in a routine quicker, and you have a shorter week when you start — you have three days, so everybody's not dead by Friday."
She said a 4-day first day of school "doesn't sound like a lot, but it's a lot."
Winter break begins with a half-day Friday, Dec. 20, and students returning to school Jan. 7.
"A hard shutdown over winter break for two solid weeks" would result in reduced heating costs and "significant savings" during "the hardest budget year we're going to have," Simmons said.
The post-Labor Day calendar would have had students returning Thursday, Jan. 2, 2025.
"This might not be a popular thing to say, but the reality is not a whole lot is going to get done on that Thursday and Friday," DiGiacomo said.
Other factors influencing the pre-Labor Day start were academic quarter dates and required parent-teacher conferences, which "we talked about ad nauseum," Simmons said.
Calling the process "wonky" and comparing it to a game of dominoes, Simmons explained the factors that prompted the calendar committee to go through "seven or eight drafts to get down to the two that made the most sense."
For example, the first quarter parent-teacher conference day will occur Nov. 5, even though it's election day, because the first quarter ends Nov. 8 and the conference day "has to fall before the first report card goes out, before grades are secured," Simmons said.
The adopted calendar has four inclement weather days built in. If they are not used, they come off the calendar.
State law, teacher contracts, mandatory conferences, state testing days, a set number of half-days, a mid-year transition day all dictate certain days off. Once all of the days off are built in, "it becomes a game of counting to 90 twice" to achieve a state-mandated 180-day school year, Simmons said.
DiGiacomo recommended surveying students next year and considering staggered starts for sixth grade and ninth grade students as they change schools.
"The pluses of draft two are just not as many as the pluses in draft one," said Rick Barton, president of the school board.
Although he liked "the idea of a longer break," school board Vice President Mark Jones was ambivalent.
"I honestly don't like either one of them, really," he said.
That ambivalence was reflected in the overall survey results, with 54% of all respondents preferring a post-Labor Day start and 46% going with the pre-Labor Day calendar.
Anticipating mixed reactions from the public and staff as well, Jones asked, "When do we want to hear complaints? Do we want to hear them right before the first day of school, or do we want to hear them after Christmas break? I think I'd probably rather hear them at the beginning of the year and get it out of the way."
To view the 2024-2025 CCPS school year calendar, visit www.carolineschools.org/page/ccps-school-calendar. The calendars are available in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole.

title: Thompson voted interim DCPS superintendent
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Thompson voted interim DCPS superintendent

 February 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Board of Education voted to appoint Jymil Thompson as interim superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools at a Board meeting Thursday.Thompson, who has been assistant superintendent since September, will serve the final months of David Bromwell's term as superintendent.
"I'm humbled and I'm appreciative and I'm gracious that you have afforded me this opportunity," Thompson, who led the Board meeting Thursday, said. "I don't take this lightly, and I want to make sure that I do the best job that I can do."
Thompson stressed that this is not a one-person job.
"I need the whole district to help," he said. "I need the whole district to collaborate with each other."
Thompson — who came to Dorchester County in 2017, serving as assistant principal and then principal at Mace's Lane Middle School until 2020 — called Dorchester County "a diamond in the rough," saying that it will take a village to get the district moving in the right direction.
"Not saying that we aren't, and (that) we haven't made some progress," he said. "But I still think we've got some ways to go in order to make sure that we move from 23rd to the top-tier school district in Maryland."
On Feb. 16, the Board of Education announced that Bromwell would not be seeking reappointment when his term ends on June 30. A week later, on Wednesday, Feb. 21, the Board announced that Bromwell would be stepping down from his position, effective March 1.
Bromwell was officially appointed as superintendent in 2020 with a four year term. Before that, he served as interim superintendent for the district. In his time at DCPS, he has also served as a teacher in the district and as the principal of Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.
According to the Feb. 21 statement from the Board of Education, the decision for Bromwell to step down in March was "mutually decided" by him and the Board. In the Feb. 16 statement, the Board expressed gratitude to Bromwell for his years of service to DCPS.
Valerie Goff, DCPS communication and community outreach specialist, said Bromwell, who was not present at the Board meeting Thursday, had no comments at this time.
At the meeting, Board Vice President Susan Morgan acknowledged that the district is experiencing change "once again."
"But I do trust in our teachers, our administrators, our directors and, now, our interim superintendent, to keep us moving forward," she said. "Through everything we as a Board do, we always keep in the front of our minds what's best for all the children that we serve."
Board Member Chris Wheedleton said the search for the district's next leader can't happen without "recognizing the value of somebody who has given close to 40 years of service to the district."
"I want to thank Mr. Bromwell for his service and for what he has done," Wheedleton said.
Earlier in the meeting, Milton Nagel and Bill Middleton from the Maryland Association of Boards of Education presented on what to keep in mind when conducting a superintendent search.
Nagel told the Board that although it was not their reason for attending the meeting, MABE does conduct superintendent searches for its member districts.
"If the Board so desires to engage in that conversation about potentially having MABE do a search, we can certainly facilitate that," he said.
In a statement released later that night, the Board said it will begin the search for a new superintendent to take office July 1.
Toward the end of his remarks at the meeting Thursday, Thompson, who is also a board member of the Talbot County Board of Education, told the public that they will get mad at him.
"But I want you to also understand this — and I mean this from the bottom of my heart — that I'm always going to make the best decisions that I think are right for kids," he said.

 Washington College's Center for Environment and Society (CES) announces the grand opening of MuSE: A Community Museum, in downtown Chestertown. The space, located at 210 S. Cross Street, will host a number of rotating exhibits highlighting Washington College teaching, experiential learning, and research with opportunities for sharing, learning, and dialogue in a community space.Each exhibit will be informational, interactive, and highly visual, creating a dynamic space for learning and sharing for the Eastern Shore community.
"Facilitating shared knowledge and understanding to drive action for conservation and community resilience is at the core of our mission," said Valerie Imbruce, director of Washington College's Center for Environment and Society. "This new off-campus space will aid us in creating opportunities for active collaboration for both teaching and learning for our Washington College community, community organizations, regional K-12 educators, students, and interested visitors. We're excited to welcome the community into this new, innovative, and collaborative space."
Last fall, the Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnerships Project was the first collaborative effort featured in the Cross Street space, which hosted a collection of exhibits created by students from five museums in Kent County — Sumner Hall, The Waterman's Museum, The Worton Point Schoolhouse, Betterton Heritage Museum, and Kent Museum. With the goal of preserving and providing greater access to the local histories of our community, the exhibition highlighted the mission of the space by providing digitized looks into each museum, viewable through virtual reality with 360-degree virtual tours, digitized collections, oral history interviews, and interactive panels.
Opening on March 1, the first exhibit in the new, updated, and enhanced space will be "Teaching & Transformation: Semester in the Chesapeake Classroom." It will showcase the nature and culture of the Chesapeake Bay region through the final projects created by Washington College's Chesapeake Semester students. Their hand-drawn maps, visual journals, and other writing and visual arts will provide visitors a sense of the unique Chesapeake ecosystem, analyze solutions to environmental problems, and explore the nexus between science, policy, and people's everyday lives in the region.
"The Chesapeake Semester is such a unique opportunity afforded to Washington College by our location here on the historically, culturally, and ecologically rich Eastern Shore," said Sara Clarke-De Reza, education department chair and director of the museum, field, and community education minor. "This exhibit showcases our students' intensive interdisciplinary study of the Chesapeake Bay, and their comparative study in watershed communities in northern Belize. The students' hope for this exhibit is that it will highlight the lessons learned through classroom and field-based experiences across the semester in a way that expands visitors' understanding of the human and social dimensions of environmental issues in our region."
When exhibits are installed, MuSE will be open on First Fridays from 4:30-7 p.m. and on Saturdays from 8 a.m. to noon during the Chestertown Farmers Market. Requests for group showings will also be available. "Teaching & Transformation: Semester in the Chesapeake Classroom" will remain open through August 2024. title: Books rife with sexual content
author: Staff Writer
content:
Books rife with sexual content

 March 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When I first heard about the "Freedom to Read" Act, Maryland SB 0738, I was reminded of the words of one of our founders, John Adams : "Liberty cannot be preserved without a general knowledge among the people, who have a right … and a desire to know; but besides this, they have a right, an indisputable, unalienable, indefeasible, divine right to that most dreaded and envied kind of knowledge, I mean of the characters and conduct of their rulers." (A Dissertation on the Canon and Feudal Law, 1765)So when I heard of the "Freedom to Read" Act, I wondered what banned books were suddenly going to be made available to the students of Maryland. I assumed there must be some politically controversial books from the Cold War Era that had been suppressed.
It was disappointing when I discovered that the books which Maryland students are being encouraged to read are rife with graphic sexual content, ones which most parents deem inappropriate for their children. Last fall, parents in Carroll County questioned why books with graphic sexual imagery were being made available to children without parental knowledge or consent.
One is the autobiography of Jaycee Dugard, who was kidnapped and used as a sex-slave in a cellar for years. I have read Dugard's "A Stolen Life: A Memoir;" it as a story of heroism but only for mature readers since it is about a kidnapping and child rape. It does not belong in a school.
An article in the Easton Gazette (Feb. 2, 2024) provides details about the "banned" books which SB 0738 is intended to liberate. To quote: "These books have pornographic images or descriptions, the likes of which you could find in Penthouse magazine. The Carroll County Board considered the opinions of parents with children as young as elementary school who complained that these books demonstrating various types of sex such as oral, vaginal, anal, etc. were accessible to students. Some of the books portrayed graphic rape scenes or sexual experimentation in the story lines that were not appropriate for any minor child."
So when Maryland schools are struggling to achieve basic literacy, how is it helpful to have students' minds filled with images of rape, etc? Why are the wishes of parents ignored and disrespected? What is the agenda?
MARY-EILEEN RUSSELL
Talbot County Republican Central Committee
Claiborne

title: Dyer achieves Eagle Scout

Dyer achieves Eagle Scout

 519
 Words

 ST. MICHAELS — A crowd of family, politicians, civic leaders and Boy Scouts assembled in the Scout House on St. Mary's Square to present the Eagle Scout Badge to Vincent Thomas Dyer Sunday.Multiple candles were lit to commemorate different aspects of his journey that started when he was 5. This is the highest honor a Scout can achieve and only about four in 100 Scouts reach it.
Dyer's sash had 26 merit badges on it, and his final project was raising $2,000 to raise a flag pole honoring veterans in Cordova. Of course, this achievment took hours of input from his family, his Troop 741 leaders and his fellow Scouts.
"It is now time to formally present you with Scouting's highest badge of accomplishment. The symbol of your success is the Eagle Scout badge and neckerchief, which will now be presented by your parents," Scoutmaster Brendan Beers said.
One of the most touching moments was when his parents, Paul and Kimberly, attached the Eagle Scout pin. He then attached pins on them for being a supportive Eagle Scout mom and dad.
Vincent's brother Paul Jr., also an Eagle Scout, said, "What does the rank of Eagle Scout represent? To me it represents saying you are going to do something and then doing it. It represents goals realized, focus and strength of character. When the pressure is on and others would run around and panic, the Eagle Scout stays calm, cool and collected in the face of atrocity."
Another person who was there to guide and bear witness is Steve Bealefeld, assistant scoutmaster.
He said, "He is a hard-working young man who has always had his head on straight."
Vincent's father listed many of the places the Scout troop went to go camping like the C & O Canal, Dorchester County and Tennessee. The biggest test was a 10-day hike at Philmont in New Mexico.
There was a testament to Vincent's leadership in the field. He was said to be an excellent cook with a Dutch oven. He can make peach cobbler and chicken pot pie.
"When he was in the lead, you were never going in the wrong direction. In the spartan wilds of Philmont, this was no small feat. Vincent is an excellent navigator. Vincent's attitude was equally as unflagging as his physical stamina. There is a deep keeled steadiness to his emotional thermostat," scout leader JoRoy Lizewski said.
Then it was time for the politicians to offer large citations. President of Town of St. Michael's Commission David Breimhurst, Del. Tom Hutchison (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), community liaison to Andy Harris Mike Detmer and Maryland state Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke briefly. Vincent was given the United States flag and the Maryland Flag.
Vincent had the last word.
"I am so proud. I am happy that all my friends from 190 and 741 were here to celebrate this event with me, because it has been a long time coming. It is a bittersweet moment. I am glad I got Eagle Scout, but I will miss Scouting as a whole," Vincent said.
He tentatively has plans to attend University of Maryland at College Park in the fall.

title: The Navy’s 'best kept secret'
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
The Navy’s 'best kept secret'

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 815
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GRASONVILLE — "Do your best. Remember to breathe. Remember why you are here.''On Saturday, March 2, this encouragement echoed through an almost silent room at the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 7464 in Grasonville during the annual inspection for the Maryland Division of the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps. While many 10 to 18 year olds relax at home on a rainy Saturday morning, 21 Sea Cadets and eight League Cadets stood at attention.
Their uniforms carefully pressed and prepared, shoes shined and haircuts and hairstyles well groomed according to the set regulations. They were prepared and ready for their yearly inspection.
The purpose of annual inspection is to prepare for combat. Although these young men and women are not going into combat, they are preparing to be productive citizens now while also preparing to be future leaders who positively impact the world around them.
Many do not know about this extraordinary program. But, some call it "the Navy's best kept secret."
Established in 1958 by the Secretary of the Navy, the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps are comprised of young men and women aged 10 through 18.
There are two programs within Sea Cadets, the Navy League Cadet Corps for middle school students aged 10 to 13, and the Naval Sea Cadet Corps for ages 13 through the end of high school.
Through the program, values of discipline, accountability and teamwork are instilled, giving cadets a chance to step outside of their comfort zones and helping them thrive.
Today, the corps has 380 units and 9,000 enrolled. Although this program is supported by both the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, the goal is not to recruit for the military but to create respectable citizens in life — no matter what their career path may be.
Lt. Maryjoe Phillips, Sea Cadet Corps supply, finance and division officer, explains that she started with this program about 10 years ago as a "drop off mom," when she would drop her daughter off to the Sea Cadet program.
Not knowing much about the Sea Cadet program, Phillips was recruited by the master chief to help.
Ten years later, she is one of the driving forces behind this Sea Cadet unit.
"The program means a lot because we are turning out really great young men and women that are going to be beneficial to our society," Phillips said. "We are raising patriots, which this country needs so badly."
She called the program "a breath of fresh air."
"With some of the turmoil going on in the world, I have seen these Cadets do some really amazing things," Phillips said. "I get so proud of them even though they are not my children. I'm amazed at what can be done."
Starting with only five cadets in 2018, the program has grown to 29 cadets and is still growing.
In April 2018, the Maryland Unit formed and was commissioned in May 2022. Before this unit formed, many parents drove their children over the bridge to Annapolis for drills and training.
Kent Island High School senior, Evan Newcomer, explained how he started his Sea Cadet training as a League Cadet in Annapolis at age 10. His parents said there were many families traveling back and forth at that time.
Newcomer's parents asked to bring this program to Maryland's Eastern Shore. He now leads as a Naval Sea Cadet Corps petty officer second class.
His experience as a League Cadet and Sea Cadet has helped grow him into the leader he is now.
"I always had a dream of serving," Newcomer said, "and I knew the military was always appealing to me. And the whole mission of all the branches was something that kind of shined to me. My uncle was a Naval Academy Grad. He inspired me to pursue that course as well as the other, older cadets in the program. (They) impressed me and made me want to pursue that dream."
After Saturday's inspection finished, the unit and their families celebrated Evan's acceptance to West Point as a life sciences major studying pre-med.
Cadets and families come from Centreville, Easton, St. Michaels, Prince Frederick and everywhere in between, as the Maryland unit is the only unit on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
Interested young persons ages 10-17 can join a drill weekend to learn more about the program. The unit is looking for adults that can give trainings (gun safety, medical and public safety) or help develop a new marksmanship program. title: Student building projects impress judges
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Student building projects impress judges

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 624
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A loud cheer arose as the team from Wicomico County Public Schools was announced as the gold cup winner in the architecture, construction and engineering competition held this week at Sts. Peter and Paul High School.The team's project was a plan for a Salisbury Riverfront Community Center and included site logistics, design, cost estimates and timelines to pitch their vision for a center on the Wicomico River.
"The judges were blown away by the projects," Judge James Cook said. "The industry is alive and well given what we have seen tonight."
What the judges saw were project proposals by four teams. In addition to the Wicomico County team, Easton, Sts. Peter and Paul, and St. Michaels high schools competed for the gold cup and scholarships.
This was the 20th annual competition for ACE Mentors, a group of professionals representing the architecture, construction and engineering industries.
Each team took the stage and pitched the case for their projects with slideshows.
The winning Wicomico project included landscape architecture and community art. The team presented the codes they would have to satisfy to create their building.
Andrea Suk, Wicomico county coordinator, was thrilled with her students' win.
"We have 15 full time students," she said. "These students are very interested in either architecture, construction or engineering."
The team worked with professional mentors in each of the ACE fields, mentors who volunteered their time to work with students.
"They give up their time to go into the schools and teach students about each of those fields and how they work together to create all the wonderful buildings and structures around us," Suk said.
The event was sponsored in part by the late Charles H. Thornton, a renowned structural engineer, educator and mentor who died in December. There were 26 other sponsors at different levels. The named scholarships were Easton Utilities, DBF/ACE Gerald Friedel Legacy, Lane Engineering, Griffith Family and CT Darnell Construction.
The platinum sponsors were the Whiting-Turner Contracting Co. and Willow Construction.
The St. Michaels High School project proposed a harbor floodgate to address global warming and the resulting flooding in town. The students proposed building a concrete wall with a 40-foot gate to let boats pass. The wall would go across the mouth of the harbor facing the Miles River.
Easton High students proposed a tourist-friendly oyster hatchery called Project Clarity in Easton Point Park. Part of their plan was to bring oysters back to that part of Easton Point.
The last project, presented by the Sts. Peter and Paul team, proposed building a castle in Wye Mills near the intersection of U.S. Route 50 and state Route 404. The castle would host jousting and mixed martial arts programming. The colossal structure was estimated to cost more than $80 million to build.
"Our project is 'The Castle,'" said Peter Anderson, a senior at Saints Peter and Paul. "I really wanted to push the boundaries of ACE and break the mold and push the boundaries. I thought a castle would be big, bold and abrasive."
The presentations were reviewed by three judges — James Cook, vice president and project manager at Rauch; Aaron Goller, a civil engineer at Easton Utilities; and Rick VanEmburgh, engineer for the Town of Easton.
Local engineer Sean Callahan is the president of Lane Engineering and a mentor in the ACE program.
"ACE mentors does a tremendous job of bringing young folk up and showing them the ropes," Callahan said. "It is great to see young folks get excited, and that is a part of what this is."
Another mentor working with students is Rebecca Saduk, a civil engineer for Easton Utilities.
"I wish I had had a program like ACE, and that is why I am so passionate about being a mentor," she said. "These kids are learning real life work habits and how to work as a team."

title: No one knows how to pay for Maryland's massive education reform
author: CAPITAL NEWS SERVICE
content:
No one knows how to pay for Maryland's massive education reform

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CAPITAL NEWS SERVICE | Section: State News 
 
 1537
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland's Democratic-led legislature passed the Blueprint for Maryland's Future in 2021, vowing to pour billions of dollars into the state's public schools to offer universal pre-K, improve teaching and make sure students are ready for college or careers.But the General Assembly didn't outline a long-term plan to fund the ambitious 10-year education reform effort — which increasingly looks like a blueprint for red ink.
The Local News Network at the University of Maryland found that the Blueprint is already devouring hundreds of millions annually from the state's fund balance, which is on target to be fully drained in 2027.
And according to a state Department of Legislative Services fiscal briefing released in January, the state will start running a structural deficit in fiscal year 2025 that will multiply nearly sixfold by fiscal year 2029, when it will hit $2.93 billion. Not coincidentally, that fiscal briefing estimates implementing the Blueprint will cost more than $4 billion in 2029.
The General Assembly's plan for dealing with the cost crunch? There isn't one — at least not yet. Neither Gov. Wes Moore in his State of the State address nor any of the Democratic state legislators interviewed for this story have offered any potential solutions for the coming Blueprint cash crunch.
"Several years from now we're going to have to have a much more direct conversation about the long-term costs," said state Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Democrat from Baltimore City. "But we're not there yet."
Republicans, meanwhile, see the Blueprint as a budget-breaker.
"We cannot pay these billions and billions of dollars in extra monies — not just state but local as well," said House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany). "We can't pay for them unless you're going to talk about new taxes — and significant taxes."
The Blueprint's background
In 2016, then-Gov. Larry Hogan and the General Assembly created the Commission on Innovation and Excellence in Education to assess the public education system in Maryland and determine whether current funding schemes were conducive to student success.
Headed by William Kirwan, the former chancellor of the University System of Maryland, the commission came to the conclusion that an overhaul was needed.
"One of the 'aha' moments of the commission was really to face the fact that in Maryland, on what we call the Nation's Report Card, Maryland's score was about in the middle … and moving in the wrong direction," said Rachel Hise, executive director of the Blueprint's Accountability and Implementation Board, a state entity that's making sure school districts adhere to the plan.
But Hogan had an "aha" moment of his own after Democrats crafted the Kirwan Commission's report into comprehensive legislation. In 2019, Hogan criticized the pending reform proposal, telling a group of county officials it would mean "billions and billions more in mandated spending increases for county and state taxpayers," according to The Frederick News-Post.
Hogan vetoed the bill creating the Blueprint in May 2020, saying he did not want to raise taxes amid the COVID-19 pandemic to fund the education plan. The General Assembly overrode his veto in 2021.
And the following year, voters elected a strong backer of the Blueprint — Democrat Wes Moore — to succeed Hogan, who is now running for a U.S. Senate seat.
On the first day of the current legislative session that began in January, Moore said he believes in the reform plan and he will work with the General Assembly to ensure the Blueprint is implemented properly and sustainably.
"I believe in the premise and the promise of the Blueprint. I think we need a world-class education system in the state of Maryland," Moore said. "I think that's going to be a prerequisite for us to be able to accomplish the economic goal that we're hoping for."
Lofty goals
In the state's 24 public school districts, the Blueprint and its lofty goals are already beginning to take shape.
Each school district has already drawn up a preliminary plan for how it will meet targets for offering pre-K, increasing teacher salaries and improving student performance. The Accountability and Implementation Board has approved all those plans after first asking for revisions.
The Blueprint is meant to revamp the state's education system by presenting the same opportunities for all students. With a law like the Blueprint, one size has to fit all to achieve its goals of maximizing reading and math skills, as well as increasing pathways into college, said Sen. Jim Rosapepe (D-Prince George's and Anne Arundel).
"So we want that for every kid across the state. We don't want variation of those goals," Rosapepe said. "Now, the details of how stuff is paid for — I mean, I think that's a conversation that will be ongoing."
Cheryl Bost, president of the Maryland State Education Association, said the teachers union is fully behind the Blueprint.
"We have a shared understanding that our goal is for students to succeed academically and become valuable citizens in our state and in our country," Bost said. "In order to do that, we have to make an investment in public education. I think for the most part, the Blueprint identifies where that money has to go."
What it doesn't do, however, is identify where the money will come from. Bost, whose union represents 74,000 educators in the state, acknowledged the concerns about the Blueprint's cost. But she indicated the increased spending on education is both needed and long overdue.
"We constitutionally have to provide a public education for all students, so the investment is needed," Bost said. "And when some people balk at, 'Oh, it's all this money' — well, we've been starving public education for many years."
The budget dilemma
The Blueprint remains fully funded in Moore's latest fiscal year 2025 budget proposal, leaving many lawmakers to turn their attention to other legislative issues this year. Ferguson, the Senate president, said in terms of current Blueprint funding, "we're more than fine."
But that's not so in the long term. The cost of implementing the Blueprint is projected to grow from $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2024 to $4.1 billion five years later, according to the Department of Legislative Services.
Meanwhile, the state's structural budget gap is set to balloon every year through 2029 — when Legislative Services expects it to be $2.9 billion and the Moore administration says it will be about $3.5 billion.
Closing that budget gap will be immensely difficult, said Christopher Summers, president and CEO of the conservative Maryland Policy Institute, who also said the Blueprint should be paused.
"Raising taxes (is) not going to solve this problem, and I think the governor knows that," said Summers, who has been critical of the Blueprint for years.
The Blueprint calls on school districts to increase education funding too, thereby prompting Summers to say that county budgets face the biggest fiscal threat.
But in Annapolis, lawmakers from both parties acknowledged that the General Assembly will have to make some tough decisions in the years to come as the Blueprint's bills come due.
"I think we know the reality that we're facing. And I think there's gonna be a lot of discussion about that," said State Sen. Guy J. Guzzone, a Democrat from Howard County. "I just don't know that there's an immediate answer."
One obvious solution would be raising taxes to cover the state's coming shortfalls. But Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey, a Republican from the Eastern Shore, said a solution lies in cutting back the demands of the Blueprint rather than paying for the sweeping overhaul as it stands.
"Republicans have stated very often that we need to move to a 'Blueprint lite' or you know, some type of education reform that takes some of the important components of the Blueprint, but at the same time is affordable and allows counties to make decisions on which parts of the Blueprint are more meaningful in each of their public school systems," Hershey said.
Democrats, however, back the current Blueprint, despite its cost. Del. Ben Barnes, a Democrat who chairs the Appropriations Committee, said legislators should start talking about a long-term payment plan for the Blueprint now. The shared values between the legislature and the governor will bring them together, Barnes said, to solve the Blueprint budget dilemma.
"This legislature, the governor, we share values, and those shared values include all the priorities of the Blueprint," Barnes said. "Getting to children who live in communities of poverty, taking care of special needs students, I mean, these are what we all ran on. And so I feel confident we'll find the revenue we need to support that program."
Several state officials have said they are looking to the Accountability and Implementation Board to issue recommendations regarding the Blueprint's budget challenges. The board has made policy proposals included in bills that, if passed this legislative session, would make adjustments to the law without changing the finances.
In addition, the board is set to release additional recommendations this legislative session.
"What the AIB has tried to sort of suggest is like, let's try to implement it the way it's intended. And if it doesn't work, if it's just no longer the right thing to do, then we need to change it," said Hise, the board's executive director. "But for many things, we haven't gotten to that point yet."
Capital News Service reporters Kiersten Hacker, Christina Walker and Ela Jalil wrote this article.

title: Target team will not see expansion this season
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Target team will not see expansion this season

 March 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 569
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Shawn Connolly, head coach for the Kent Island Clay Target Team, presented updates and hopes for expansion to the Queen Anne's Board of Education during their regular meeting March 6.Connolly celebrated the the team, who was featured in the fall issue of PullUSA Magazine.
Several of the students, along with Connolly, were interviewed for the national publication that is distributed to 36,000 students around the country in 37 states, he said. The Kent Island team is recognized as being the first public school in Maryland to join the USA High School Clay Target League.
"It was very cool to see ourselves in the spotlight," he said.
Connolly appeared before the board this month to seek approval to expand the team's student limit to accommodate growing interest in the sport.
School team limits are typically based on funding, transportation, or the nature of the sport, none of which are applicable in the target team's case, noted Connolly.
The team is self funded and participates at a private facility with all transportation, sponsorship and insurance covered, he said.
"I'm just trying to provide this sport to as many as I can," he added.
Connolly noted the official league rules mandate a ratio of 10 students to one coach, and he has personally mandated even more strict requirements, with one coach for every squad of five students.
Now the team currently has six all-volunteer coaches, "And we have many more that would be willing to help out, and there are always parents," he said.
All students are welcome to the target team no matter their athletic ability; it allows students to wear a uniform and be a part of team who might not otherwise, Connolly said.
"One of the beauties of this league is that everybody participates," without tryouts and slots available only for the most skilled students, he said. However, students must pass a safety program and register before they participate.
Last year the team turned away about five students due to capacity, he said.
As team capacity falls under the superintendent's authority, the board turned to Superintendent Patricia Saelens, who noted Queen Anne's County was the only public school district in Maryland that offered clay target teams as an engaging extracurricular activity, not to mention scholarship opportunities.
Saelens thanked Connolly for his leadership and passion to bring the sport to students, but said at this time the district will not be expanding the program.
"I think we are very blessed and very lucky that we have had this opportunity in this district," she said.
The Queen Anne's School District is insured through the Maryland Association of Boards of Education (MABE), and although the target team covers its own insurance, the MABE attorney has cautioned districts against expanding target teams due to affiliation that could potentially expose districts to potential risk and litigation.
Currently Queen Anne's County School District pays an increased premium for any firearms within the district, including school resource officers funded through the Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Department, according to Saelens.
MABE will be meeting again in April to consider revisions and amendments, including potentially increasing premiums, she said.
At the moment, the district will keep the team limit as it is and wait to see how the MABE discussion unfolds.
Connolly said he understood the decision and thanked the board and superintendent for their time.
The Queen Anne's County Board of Education will next meet for a work session March 20 at 5 p.m. and hold a regular meeting April 10 at 6 p.m.

title: TCPS looks into creation of clay target shooting club
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
TCPS looks into creation of clay target shooting club

 March 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 562
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Board of Education is hoping to make a decision in May regarding a request for a high school clay target shooting club.At a Board of Education meeting Wednesday, the board heard from five members of the public asking that it approve the creation of the club. The board also heard from Talbot County Public Schools Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones about the district's research into whether this club could be created at TCPS.
During public comment, Sheriff Joe Gamble spoke on behalf of the Talbot County Sheriff's Office about the importance of having a space for a group of teens to come together and be a part of something.
"We all know kids want to be a part of a group, they want to be a part of something," he said. "The Sheriff's Office fully supports another venue for our youth to connect with other people of like-minded and like interests."
Austin Eader, a ninth grader at Easton High School, said that this week he gathered 191 student signatures and 24 teacher and staff signatures from people who support having the club.
Many of people interested in starting the club, including Talbot Rod & Gun Club President Joe Capozzoli, spoke at a board meeting in October requesting approval to create the club.
After that meeting, TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi instructed her staff to look into what it would take to make the club happen. At the meeting Wednesday, Assistant Superintendent for Curriculum and Instruction Helga Einhorn said Jones has been leading that charge.
Jones told the board that the district has been meeting with those interested in starting the club to gather more information. She said the biggest concern right now is figuring out if the club could in any way jeopardize the district financially — particularly from a risk management perspective.
She said that although they have heard about the training and safety precautions required to participate in the program, it still involves putting a firearm in students' hands.
"We have to be very thoughtful about that," she said.
The district has gone to its insurance provider, the Maryland Association of Boards of Education Group Insurance Pool. Jones said a discussion around the topic was held at a February MABE meeting, and MABE intends to hold a session and vote on this at its annual meeting in late April.
Jones said the district will need to consider whether MABE will continue to provide liability coverage if an incident were to happen and, if so, whether it would be at an additional cost. She said the district doesn't have these answers yet because MABE hasn't voted on it yet.
Jones said she should have these answers for the May Board of Education meeting.
Board President Emily Jackson said the board and district are at MABE's mercy at this point. She said that as long as MABE has this discussion in April, the board should be able to make a firm decision in May regarding the creation of the club.
At the end of the meeting, board member Deborah Bridges said she is on board with the creation of the team.
"I think it would be a wonderful addition to our county," she said. "I think it's important because girls can do it too. And there's limited access for females these days. And also for the children that can't do regular athletics, because they can be a part of it too."

title: Jymil Thompson resigns from Talbot County Board of Education
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Jymil Thompson resigns from Talbot County Board of Education

 March 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 311
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Jymil Thompson has resigned from his District 1 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education.At a board meeting Wednesday, Board President Emily Jackson announced the news of Thompson's resignation.
"Our wonderful Dr. Jymil Thompson has been forced to resign his seat on the board as he was appointed interim superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools," she said.
Jackson said the board will miss him and wishes him the best of luck in his new position.
Last month, the Dorchester County Board of Education voted to to appoint Jymil Thompson as interim superintendent of DCPS. He is serving the final months of David Bromwell's term as superintendent. Bromwell officially stepped down from the position March 1.
Before taking on the role of interim superintendent, Thompson served as assistant superintendent for DCPS. He began that role in September.
Thompson, who was sworn in to the Talbot County Board of Education in December of 2022, said in an interview that he will miss working on the Talbot County Board of Education.
"I've always been on the other side of the fence in relation to education," he said. "But on the board side, I learned a lot about policy, budgeting and things of that nature. So it was a very valuable experience."
He said his experience as a board member is beneficial to his new role as interim superintendent, particularly when it comes to understanding the relationship between a superintendent and board of education.
TCPS Executive Assistant Charlene Gould said Thursday that the governor's office has been notified of the District 1 vacant seat. The governor's office is responsible for appointing someone to fill that seat until Thompson's term expires in 2026.
Thompson said his advice for whoever fills his seat is to listen.
"I just learned to listen," he said about when he started on the board. "And then make decisions after I listened to what people had to say."

author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Rotary event encourages students to explore local jobs, careers

 March 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — Local Rotary Clubs welcomed high school students for a day of opportunities and exploration with the third annual Career Day at Chesapeake College on March 15.Understanding that not all students will go to college or join the military, the Centreville Rotary Club and the Rotary Club of Kent Island once again sponsored a career day at Chesapeake College hosting students from Queen Anne's County High, Kent Island High and Wye River Upper School to discover potential careers.
Event organizer Doug Storck of the Centreville Rotary Club welcomed the opportunity to partner with Chesapeake College and highlight the surrounding businesses that students may not have ever considered for employment opportunities. The day is always well received by students and organizations alike, he said.
Career coaches work with students throughout the year to identify those who would most benefit from the program, he said.
Storck was grateful for the collaboration and thanked the high school administration for leading the way for their students to be on the track to greatness.
"They are here because they care about the success of their students," he said.
Throughout the day of career discovery, students received one on one individual learning opportunities from professionals through mock interviews and financial guidance workshops.
Chesapeake College also presented information on what vocational classes can do for career growth and continual development.
A career fair with 30 local businesses welcomed students to discover hiring opportunities and highlighted skills through a multitude of interests available to them right in their own backyard.
Founder of local IT company Corsica Technologies, guest speaker Dale Walls shared what perseverance can mean for your own story of success.
Walls recounted his own rocky childhood after which he found structure and direction in the United States Marine Corps before going on to found Corsica Technologies.
Since stepping down as CEO, Walls has continued his impressive resume, running marathons, coaching youth football and raising a family.
Encouraging students to take charge of their lives, Walls noted it was perfectly okay not to know what you wanted to do with your life as a high schooler, as long as you were moving forward trying to identify the kind of person you wanted to be.
To do that, he reiterated the importance of setting goals with clarity, having courage and leading the way for future self-success.
"You are the one who is going to get you there," he said.
The day of career exploration is very important to the Rotary Club mindset of "Service Above Self," according to Kent Island chapter President Candi Cook.
The job fair helps students explore the local area for career opportunities in one convenient place and helps eliminate the misconception that students need to leave the area to find quality jobs.
"There are plenty of opportunities for successful post-high school careers that don't require a college degree and taking on tons of debt," she said.

title: Maryland teachers learn from success in literacy labs
author: Matt Hubbard mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
Maryland teachers learn from success in literacy labs

 March 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard mhubbard@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After schools in Cecil County were identified as a top performer in student literacy growth, educators from across Maryland gathered there for a Literacy Learning Lab.The effort was hosted by Cecil County Public Schools.
The lab comes in the wake of the Maryland Department of Education identifying CCPS as third in the state for student growth on state reading and writing assessments.
The two-day Literacy Learning Lab took place at the Cecil County School of Technology where educators from a number of Maryland's 24 school districts learned about CCPS's methodologies for identifying and addressing students with additional literacy learning needs in grades four through eight.
According to school officials, these methodologies have led CCPS to not only create a system which helps all students, but they also yield results that show consistent improvement in student literacy performance — identified by the state — year over year.
"What we do is not different from the rest of the state, it is where Maryland State Department of Education wants us to be and CCPS is closer to the ideal so we are viewed as a model," said Rhonda Asplen, CCPS's Instructional Coordinator for Secondary English Language Arts Literacy.
The system CCPS uses to identify student needs is Bookworms — a program that provides teachers with resources to implement reading and writing courses.
Bookworms is used in conjunction with assessments to enable CCPS educators to accurately assess students and make data driven decisions when placing students into one of the three tiers of CCPS's multi-tier support system.
One tier is for students proficient in reading and writing skills. The second tier is for students who need additional support and the last tier is for students who struggle the most with meeting grade level literacy requirements.
CCPS works in collaboration with the Professional Development Center for Educators at the University of Delaware where officials continue to develop the multi-tier system to ensure CCPS continues to make data informed decisions when matching students with literacy learning resources.
"We want to continue the work we are acknowledged for because our kids deserve it," said CCPS's Instructional Coordinator for Elementary English Language Arts, Sherry Eichinger-Wilson.
The work of both Eichinger-Wilson and Asplen have allowed CCPS to lead the state for meeting the requirements of the 2019 Ready to Read Act, the science-based program, Science of Reading, and the College and Career Readiness portion of Blueprint for Maryland's Future — a statewide funding initiative that aims to increase education quality and funding in Maryland.
"The focus is to make sure that what we offer in our program is aligned to the Science of Reading," Eichinger-Wilson said. "We have a vertical alignment from grades K-12 and we are continuing to evaluate the parts of our program to ensure that they are aligned and that we are meeting the needs of all of our students."
Cecil and Washington County are the only two counties in the state to be deemed as Literacy Learning Lab models for leveraging student support aligned with the Science of Reading to improve literacy outcomes for students in fourth through eighth grade.
