title: An open letter on recent education mailers
author: SHARON PEPUKAYI and EMILY JACKSON Talbot County Public Schools
content:
An open letter on recent education mailers

 October 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SHARON PEPUKAYI and EMILY JACKSON Talbot County Public Schools | Section: Columns 
 
 534
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Dear Talbot County Community,We would like to address the recent mailers that have been distributed to homes throughout our community. This campaign unfairly targets our schools, students, and dedicated Talbot County Public Schools educators.
Our team does face challenges like many school districts, and we face them directly and with transparency. While we do not want to give life to these messages you are receiving, we want to make sure our community knows the truth.
We are working to improve our performance on state assessments. With support from the Talbot County Council, we have made significant investments, including acquiring new rigorous standards-based curricula and hiring and retaining qualified teachers and administrators. Additionally, we have made math one of our priorities and are putting concentrated efforts into the teaching and learning of this curricular area. We also know that student success is measured by many indicators in addition to state assessment scores.
While we know we have work to do, there is growth we can celebrate. The 23-24 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment results showed modest improvement across all Maryland districts. In Talbot County, our overall margin of progress was slightly greater than what the state achieved. In English/Language Arts, out of the 24 school districts, Talbot County Public Schools had the greatest increase in students being proficient. These results inform our continued work on the initiatives put in place to provide our educators with the resources needed to ensure student success.
We adhere to the Health Education Standards set forth by the Maryland Department of Education. Maryland state law requires that parents/guardians be notified about topics covered in the Family Life unit. They have the option of having their student excused if they are uncomfortable with this content being taught to their students by TCPS educators.
Our Talbot County students graduate from our high schools and continue to excel in college, career and life. This is a result of their hard work, the commitment of the TCPS team, the leadership of the Board of Education and the support of the County Council and our many community partners.
Our support staff, teachers and administrators are dedicated professionals who deserve our trust and support. By collaborating openly and constructively, we can ensure that our school system remains a beacon of opportunity and excellence for every child, regardless of their background.
We invite the community to our established public forums scheduled each month through our regular Board of Education meetings. These meetings are open to all citizens, and we encourage everyone to attend and participate in these sessions. Only through collaboration and communication do we truly provide the best opportunities for our students.
We are honored to serve as Talbot County's superintendent of schools and president of the Board of Education, and we are very proud of our students and staff. We believe in and will continue to advocate for TCPS students, families and educators. We are TCPS, and we are committed to transforming and performing together.
If you have questions or concerns, please email us at info@talbotschools.org. We are here for you and all of the children of Talbot County. Thank you for your continued support.
Sharon Pepukayi is the superintendent of Talbot County Public Schools. Emily Jackson is president of the Talbot County Board of Education.

title: School mailing accusations are false
author: Staff Writer
content:
School mailing accusations are false

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Talbot county residents have recently been receiving U.S. Postal Service mailings questioning the quality of teaching in our county's public schools. Among its many criticisms, the glossy mailings falsely decry the low English and math proficiency and attribute these low scores to time wasted "forcing harmful gender ideology" on students.Here are some facts: 39% of students in Talbot County are classified as "economically disadvantaged" (data gathered by US News and World Report), and 40% are members of a minority. Fully 14% of students study English as a second language. Talbot County Public Schools is one of only eight districts out of the 24 in Maryland that earned star ratings of three or higher for all schools. (reportcard.msde.maryland.gov)
In 2023 Talbot County Schools boasted an attendance rate of 91.5% and a high school graduation rate of 95%. Schools also showed year over year improvement in academic achievement. These are numbers to be proud of, not scorned.
So where are these accusations and false claims coming from? They are originating from a group identifying itself as "Pay Attention America Inc." with a postal address listed as 1000 N. West St, Suite 1200, Wilmington, Delaware. In its mailings, it cites the "Daily Citizen" whose director of communications claims: "God has declared certain things 'good' and certain things 'bad.' He's given us clear principles to use in considering current events. And He's spoken clearly on the subjects of life, marriage, law and government. We cannot remain morally neutral in our reporting."
Are we all to believe that God has spoken directly to the Daily Citizen and told it what is good and what is bad and facts are irrelevant? The mailings scream "radical politicians are pushing extreme radical agendas" and "radical indoctrination" of children is taking place in the schools.
Unfortunately, our public schools make an easy target for out of state organizations with a defined political agenda. It is sad that their misrepresentations and slurs seek to divide our community instead of seeking solutions in a positive, fact-based approach. We believe it is important, more now than ever, to make decisions based on facts, not gobbledygook.
Ultimately, we question why a Delaware religious organization finds it necessary to alarm us when all Talbot citizens have to do is simply talk to our teachers and our school administrators about our concerns.
That is how local control works.
JIM WILKINS
MARTHA HAMLYN
JIM RICHARDSON
Claiborne

title: Decline in social capital has reached new lows
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Decline in social capital has reached new lows

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Almost 25 years ago, Harvard professor and political scientist Robert Putnam wrote "Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community."In it, Putnam provides a detailed analysis of a measurable decline starting in 1950 of what he calls "social capital" in American society. Putnam also discusses the very serious consequences of that decline.
Putnam suggests these consequences include, but are not limited to disengagement from community involvement, decreased voter turnout, low attendance at public meetings, and shrinking memberships in fraternal groups, civic organizations and political parties. Putnam also cited Americans' growing distrust in their government. He maintains all of these consequences undermines the active civic engagement which a democracy requires from its citizens.
Since his book was published, I suggest the decline in social capital in America has reached new low levels, due in large part to long term limited social interactions during the covid pandemic.
This has been especially the case with regards to young children in their formative years (ages birth through age 8) when their brains are most active in the development of how they communicate and interact with the world.
As I write this commentary, I am in a state of shock about an incident at the Oct. 25 Talbot County GOP Lincoln Reagan Dinner. While the guest speaker was delivering his remarks, he was confronted which led to an arrest and assault charge against the confronting individual.
This occurrence brings back memories of World War II when German Nazis threatened the principles of civil discourse, free speech and the democratic governance principles of western society. They came very close to invading Britain which would have almost guaranteed Britain's surrender and a different end to an epic global struggle between good and evil.
During those dark days, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill was a master at rallying the British people. During one especially challenging time when there were regular and unpredictable Nazi fire bombings of civilian targets, Churchill said, "In times of great uncertainty, look for great opportunities."
Churchill's understanding of the value of social capital and his communication skills ultimately led to Britain and Britain's allies (including the United States) winning World War II.
America is certainly facing times of great uncertainty. Now more than ever America needs a renewed commitment by our citizenry to look for great opportunities to learn about engaging in collaborative efforts to increase and maintain social capital.
A place to start is here. A time to start is now.
There are three outstanding opportunities to do so on the Eastern Shore.
The first opportunity is to read Putnam's book, which is available at the Talbot County Library.
The second opportunity is attending an upcoming program sponsored by the Chesapeake Forum, a local not-for-profit academy for lifelong learning. The program topic is — "Our lost sense of community — how do we fix it?"
This program includes three sessions to be held on Nov. 7, Nov. 14 and Nov. 21 between 10:30 a.m. and noon. All sessions are at the YMCA on Peachblossom Road in Easton. For online registration go to chesapeakeforum.org. The registration fee is $50 per person. A reduced registration fee is available. Questions? Email info@chesapeakeforum.org.
The third opportunity is a Baylor University Baylor in Washington webinar. The webinar topic is "Political Desaturation: How to Thrive Before, During and After the 2024 Election."
Webinar speakers are Robert B. Talisse, W. Alton Jones professor of philosophy and professor of political science at Vanderbilt University; Dr. Curt Thompson, psychiatrist, author and speaker; and Elizabeth Oldfield, senior fellow of the think-tank Theos and a coach and consultant working with purpose-driven individuals and organizations.
Some pertinent observations from the speakers in this free one-hour webinar include:
Get in the same room. "When human beings get in the same room as each other, they find they have acres in common." — Dr. Curt ThompsonSeek understanding over division. "We're increasingly capable of being disagreeable; but we're becoming less capable of disagreeing because it's harder to understand what another person's position actually is." — Robert TalisseRebuild. "We need to rebuild the civic infrastructure of our common life away from politics."— Elizabeth Oldfield
The entire Baylor webinar is available for viewing using the following link: washington.web.baylor.edu/events/past-events.
Some may suggest a group of Eastern Shore of Maryland residents reading Putnam's book, attending a Chesapeake Forum program and watching a Baylor University zoom meeting will not make a difference in an uncertain world.
I disagree.
Working together to expand and maintain social capital will make a difference in our community.
It can also be a much-needed step forward in our society to affirm Margaret Mead's timeless observation: "Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed, citizens can change the world. Indeed, it is the only thing that ever has."

title: Maryland conservatives make gains in school board races
author: Adam Hudacek Capital News Service
content:
Maryland conservatives make gains in school board races

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Adam Hudacek Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1263
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Conservative school board candidates saw sweeping wins across Maryland this week, defying expectations in the largely blue state and solidifying the influence of the 1776 Project PAC, the Republican-aligned organization that endorsed 19 candidates statewide.In total, 11 of the political action committee's endorsed candidates either won or narrowly led their races as of Friday morning. Candidates backed by the PAC won control of the school boards in Somerset and Calvert counties, while appearing poised to win in Talbot County. Final results await the counting of some mail-in and provisional ballots, which must be counted by Nov. 15.
Campaign finance records show that the Maryland State Education Association Fund for Children and Public Education — the political arm of the state's teachers union — spent $516,999.57 during the 2024 election cycle. And the 1776 Project PAC clearly sees the teachers' union as its defeated rival in the election.
"Even outspending us by $450,000, the teachers' union couldn't beat us in deep-blue Maryland—their message is just too extreme," said Stefano Forte, executive director of the 1776 Project PAC. "Voters chose raising test scores and graduation rates over their far-left culture war. On Tuesday, common sense won, and that has no price tag."
A fourth school district with candidates targeted for defeat by Democrats — Washington County — also flipped to conservative control without the aid of the 1776 Project PAC.
Of those 11 winners endorsed by that conservative PAC, six had also been targeted for defeat by the Maryland Democratic Party, which selected 24 "extreme" conservative school board candidates in the state to directly invest against — a move the party referred to as "unprecedented." Of those 24, only nine have been lost thus far. The remaining 15 all won or are leading their respective races.
"We are proud that we pushed out some of the most extreme elements in these races," said Luca Amayo, spokesperson for the Maryland Democratic Party. "It's clear, however, that we must continue to bolster our grassroots efforts and make Marylanders aware of the far-right agenda encroaching into Maryland's public schools, especially as they are emboldened under a Donald Trump presidency."
The party considers the 1776 Project PAC a "radical ring-wing group," and helped defeat five of its endorsed candidates from winning office. Ryan James Girdusky, the committee's founder, wrote on the PAC's website that he created the organization "to change public education by reforming school boards and electing reform-minded conservatives who wanted to improve public education in this country."
As of Oct. 16, the PAC had pumped $90,580.50 toward the campaigns of 13 candidates across Cecil, Queen Anne's, Talbot, Calvert, Somerset and St. Mary's counties.
In Calvert County, candidates endorsed by the 1776 Project PAC won all three school board seats.
Retired principal Mike Shisler lost his bid for the board. He said he fears that the new conservative leadership, all of whom were targeted by the state's Democratic Party as well, would create inequity and fear within the county's education system.
"I'm very disappointed in the results," Shisler said Wednesday, "It's not going to be inclusive of everybody. It's going to target folks. It's going to try to undo the work of previous boards of education when it came to stressing equity and diversity, and I think they're trying to roll back the clock."
Joseph Marchio, who defeated Shisler, said he expected a close race going into Tuesday night. His margin was the closest of the three 1776 Project PAC-backed victors in Calvert County.
In Washington County, on the state's panhandle, all four candidates that Democrats targeted for defeat won their election, flipping the county's school board into conservative control. All three non-targeted incumbents lost reelection, while April Ann Zentmeyer, the only targeted incumbent, defended hers.
"I look forward to working with new board members and faithful colleagues to maximize opportunities for students, faculty, staff, and parents; and to identify solutions that will strengthen WCPS," Zentmeyer said in a statement.
Washington County has a county-wide school board election process, as opposed to the school districts where candidates are elected by district. Instead of one-on-one races, all school board candidates in Washington County face each other in a crowded pool, with the top four vote-getting candidates winning seats. Carroll, Allegany and Frederick counties have similar systems.
The success of conservative school board candidates around Maryland reflects a larger trend from this year's election cycle: the state's rightward shift. According to data from the Associated Press, every county in Maryland shifted rightward this year compared to the 2020 election — from two points in Charles County and Baltimore City to eight points in Cecil County.
Some races remain too close to call. In Frederick County, two conservative candidates targeted by Democrats led the race for three seats as of Friday, but two other candidates trailed close behind. Talbot County, which flipped conservative this cycle, saw two 1776 Project PAC-endorsed candidates win seats, while a third trailed by a narrow margin as of Friday with votes still left to tally.
Somerset County, the third district flipped by 1776 Project PAC-endorsed contenders, saw massive margins of victory for the conservatives, with Mary Beth Bozman securing about four-fifths of the vote in her race. Her opponent was Alverne "Chet" Chesterfield — who, the Local News Network reported last month, had a peace order initiated against him in 2022.
The Local News Network also reported that Brandie Edelen, a 1776 Project PAC-endorsed candidate in St. Mary's County, had a state tax lien filed against her in 2019. Edelen handily lost her race to Josh Guy.
In deep-blue Howard County, Andrea Chamblee is in a tight race with Trent Kittleman, an early supporter of the county's Moms for Liberty chapter. Even though Democrat Kamala Harris carried over two-thirds of the votes cast in the presidential race in the county, Chamblee led Kittleman by only 3.5 points as of Friday morning.
Mail-in and provisional ballots, which have leaned in favor of Chamblee this far, are still being counted.
The founder of Moms for Liberty in Frederick County, Jaime Brennan, appeared headed to victory. She said that despite the Maryland Democrats' campaign against her and Colt Black, the other conservative in the race, that effort didn't appear to be all that effective.
"They spent a lot of money in opposition to me and Colt, and to prop up the other side, but I didn't hear from a single person who said, 'Oh, I heard about this and I'm not voting for you,'" Brennan said.
In neighboring Carroll County, where Moms For Liberty lobbied for the removal of 60 books from school libraries — 21 permanently — conservative candidates secured their hold on the board. Greg Malveaux and Kristen Zihmer defeated Amanda Jozkowski and Muri Lynn Dueppen, who together ran an underdog progressive campaign called the Slate for Student Success, which was endorsed by the Carroll County Educators Association.
"It's really a shame that a lot of voters in our county chose to kind of take their marching orders from their political party, rather than considering the opinions of the educators," Jozkowski said. She previously ran and lost in 2022.
Jozkowski said the race was a reflection of the national results, which saw an overwhelming rightward shift in nearly every state and in many down-ballot races. Malveaux and Zihmer were both targeted by the Maryland Democrats.
That rightward shift could also be seen in the school board race in Anne Arundel County's District 3. There, the conservative candidate, Chuck Yocum, fell only 2.76 points behind his opponent, Erica McFarland, despite weeks of controversy over Yocum's 1994 acquittal on child sexual abuse and perverted practices charges.
Local News Network reporters Sasha Allen, Marwa Barakat, Ela Jalil, Colin McNamara and Tolu Talabi contributed to this report.

title: St. Michaels temporary library opens at Village Shopping Center
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels temporary library opens at Village Shopping Center

 November 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News

 ST. MICHAELS — The Talbot County Free Library, St. Michaels Branch has opened its temporary location at the St. Michaels Village Shopping Center on Talbot Street. To celebrate the grand opening, the library provided free coffee, craft bags and donuts for all visitors on Tuesday morning.The Talbot Free Library on Fremont Street is currently undergoing construction for its building expansion. The temporary location, at the site of the former St. Michaels YMCA, will serve residents of St. Michaels until the expansion is complete.
Shauna Beulah, branch manager for the library, said construction at the Fremont location will take about a year to 18 months.
"A full service library will offer all of the services we had there, a Xerox machine, children's area with all the different kinds of materials they had, and audio books and DVDs, new books, all of those things," Beulah said.
Beulah said the location of the temporary library was important because it needed to be accessible and a familiar space for residents to visit.
Though it is a full-service library, there are some amenities the temporary location does not provide, including meeting rooms and an external book drop, so books will need to be returned during open hours.
But Beulah said the wait would be worth the vast renovation expected at the Fremont location. Renovations include an eating area, social computer rooms, a quiet reading section and a multi-purpose section for all.
Diana Hastings, youth services librarian, said the first few families who visit the new library will get a fall bag with fun crafts for all ages to encourage creativity and family-based activities.
Hastings, who is also an art therapist, said she tries to provide hands-on crafts and activities to young readers to create and explore and prepare for their journey into literacy.
Though the temporary library is a smaller space, Hastings said it provides an extensive array of youth books, including bilingual children's book, fiction, non-fiction chapter books, vox books (live print audio books) and recorded storybooks. If a book is not available at the library, librarians can order it from a different library.
This way efforts are made for residents to still have access to the information they need.
"We hope that families take advantage of coming here, utilizing our resources, and we welcome them," Hastings said.

 EASTON — Talbot County Public Schools is looking at new leadership, according to uncertified vote totals from the Maryland Board of Elections.Cynthia Marrah Jurrius, Karla Wieland-Cherry and Ann O'Connor, none of whom have prior experience on the Talbot County Board of Education, won seats for their districts.
The elected board members said they plan to bring their campaign priorities to the forefront of their terms, which begin Dec. 1 and will last for four years.
Talbot County's Board of Education is made up of seven members from different districts in the county and two student board members. Districts 2, 5 and 6 were on the ballot in the November election.
For district 2, O'Connor won with 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Board of Elections, beating out incumbent Board Member Candace Henry. O'Connor said her campaign provided the opportunity for her to get a better understanding of leading a campaign, school board responsibilities and Blueprint, Maryland's 10-year plan to improve the state's education system.
O'Connor said she has just skimmed the surface and is ready to learn more.
She said she will be prioritizing academics and discipline. With academics, she said she would like to see elementary students reading every night and working on more book reports, and for schools to provide summer reading lists.
For discipline, O'Connor said she has noticed a lack of consistency, or "different rules for different people."
"We need a plan for all the schools that this is the way we're going to, you know, this is the dress, this is the behavior when you walk in the building. If you veer from that, there's going to be this consequence, and you got to, I mean, it's the follow through," she said.
For District 5, Karla Wieland-Cherry won with 54.6% votes, according to the State Board of Elections. Wieland-Cherry, who defeated incumbent Board Member Anna Howie, said she appreciated the support she received from her campaign, though she did mention she "got a lot of negativity." She hopes she can work through any negative sentiments to have a productive four years on the board.
Wieland-Cherry said she will be prioritizing open communication for everyone she works with and promoting the Career and Technology Education Program, which offers job training in various fields.
She said it's important to encourage kids to look at career alternatives for those not interested in college, whether that be training to become a firefighter, plumber or welder.
"I think (the CTE program is) under encouraged, under utilized," Wieland-Cherry said. "And that's where jobs are."
For District 6, Jurrius won with 51.9% of the vote, defeating Kerry Gunshenan, according to the State Board of Elections. Current District 6 Board Member Mary Wheeler did not seek reelection.

title: Maryland schools get new rules for shooter drills
author: MARISSA YELENIK Capital News Service
content:
Maryland schools get new rules for shooter drills

 November 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARISSA YELENIK Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 809
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Active shooter drills in Maryland schools will be different next school year under a new set of state guidelines meant to limit the impact those drills have on the mental health of students.The new guidelines prohibit trauma-inducing elements like imitation of gunfire or explosions. They also require school systems to notify parents in advance when students will be practicing what to do in the event of an active shooter in their buildings.
The new guidelines were released by the Maryland Center for School Safety this fall, ordered by a new state law requiring them to draft new parameters and create a new process for collecting and analyzing data on their effectiveness. The center will also look into the psychological impact the shooter drills have on staff, parents and students.
Parts of the guidelines — including bans on gunfire and the requirement to notify parents — have already gone into effect because they are part of state law. The full set of guidelines will be put into effect at the beginning of the academic year in 2025.
"The mental health crisis that we see in our young people is undeniable," said Del. Jared Solomon, who sponsored the measure in the Maryland House of Delegates earlier this year. "As we normalize having to deal with school shootings, we are creating more anxiety and more issues among young people."
While schools have long practiced safety drills, active shooter drills are relatively new, following the 1999 shooting at Columbine High School, according to the guidelines.
School systems have made an effort to keep students safe by implementing active shooter drills, however, concerns have been raised across the country about the impact these drills have on student's mental health. This led to the April passage of the Maryland bill, as well as an executive order signed by President Joe Biden to increase federal guidance on the subject.
Maryland's new guidelines, released in October, call for unified terminology between districts to discourage miscommunication between the school system and the relevant public. They intend to increase communication between staff and students to create an open dialogue where everyone feels comfortable raising concerns, as well as creating a diverse planning team who will work on planning the drills and doing a post-analysis of how it went and any shortcomings it faced.
The guidelines emphasize that active shooter drills are not a one-size-fits-all matter, and should be adjusted to fit the age group.
"These are going to be part of a young person's life for the foreseeable future, but that doesn't mean that you can't do them in a way that is both trauma-informed and age-appropriate," said Solomon. "It's really important that the way school systems do these types of events reflects a care and age appropriateness of the grades that are being impacted."
The guidelines also recommend that a mechanism be established to pause or stop the drill when necessary, for schools to notify parents before and after all drills to increase trust and communication and to allow students and staff who feel uncomfortable to opt-out from the drills.
The Maryland General Assembly sponsors of the bill, Solomon and Sen. Cheryl Kagan, felt that the impact guns have on today's children needs to be mitigated as much as possible, and worked to balance a focus on their safety while prioritizing their mental health.
"The law that Del. Solomon and I sponsored and passed tried to walk the fine line of thoughtful preparation that isn't traumatic," Kagan said. "And we also had to consider parents and community members who are understandably alarmed and concerned when they see the impact of these drills … Our concern was that [the drills] were not being strategic in how they were handled, and were actually causing trauma for those involved."
One active shooter drill that occurred in Solomon's district served as a driving force for his involvement.
"Families were literally getting texts from their kids saying 'I don't know if I'll ever see you again' and it was a drill. They didn't know," said Solomon. "There was no requirement prior to this for a school or a school system to notify families before or after."
Additional drivers for the bill included shared experiences from other parents Solomon spoke to, he said. Many shared frustrations at the lack of foresight they had into when the drills would be taking place and what would happen during them, preventing them from having appropriate conversations with their children to prepare them.
Starting in January, schools will distribute a new survey made by the National Center for School Mental Health to gather feedback from staff, parents and students on how effective the drills are, and the mental impact they have on all involved.
"The goal is not to create fear but to instill confidence and preparedness," the Maryland Center for School Safety said in their guidelines. "By working together as a community, schools can foster safe and supportive learning environments."

title: Talbot County Education Foundation honors 3 alumni
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County Education Foundation honors 3 alumni

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 508
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Keasha Haythe, JoAnn Asparagus Murray and Ludwig Eglseder III were honored by Talbot County Public Schools on Friday for their contributions to the community and public education.A ceremony at the Oxford Community Center presented Haythe, Asparagus Murray and Eglseder as the district's 2024 Distinguished Alumni. It also raised funds for projects and initiatives in the school district requested by teachers.
Friday's event raised showcased six specific requests, including a student leadership program, pre-kindergarten language and literacy, and the Easton Middle School band, according to TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi.
"To me, this event is near and dear, recollecting back to my teacher days and having those really nice innovative ideas, but knowing sometimes the funding doesn't stretch," Pepukayi said. "I can resonate with the teachers being able to have these ideas, to write them up, pitch them, and then more importantly be able to talk about them to the people who can help and assist."
Haythe, who is president of the nonprofit organization Foundation of Hope and also serves on the Talbot County Council, graduated from Easton High School in 1991.
She said she remembers teachers in elementary, middle and high school who helped her believe in herself.
"Hopefully I can encourage other people to believe in themselves that may doubt themselves in high school because there's a lot of people that have it together and they're voted most likely to succeed, and then there's some others that are in high school that may not think that. They may doubt themselves," Haythe said in an interview.
Eglseder graduated from St. Michaels High School in 1975. Following medical school, He began working as a physician in Easton in 1986, and has provided internal medicine services to the community for the 38 years since.
Asparagus Murray attended Robert Russa Moton High School from seventh through 11th grade before moving to Philadelphia. From 1996 to 2022, she worked as a family law magistrate in the Caroline County District Court.
In an interview, she said her time at Moton High School and in Easton taught her how to advocate for people, a skill she carried forward to her career in social work. Asparagus Murray said Moton High School — an all-Black school at the time — was critical in her formative years.
"I think that the camaraderie and the spirit of the school is really unmatched for minority students. It's hard to describe what that was like," Asparagus Murray said. "Even though you may have been considered the step-child of the system, we never saw ourselves as that. And the faculty certainly didn't try to get us to think that that was the case. Their focus was rising above what is expected. I think that's irreplaceable."
She said Friday's recognition was an honor, adding that it's critical for people to continue supporting public education.
"No matter where you go to school or anything, we always have to have a strong public educational system, because that is the vehicle by which most of our citizenry is educated," Asparagus Murray said. " … Education is the key to unlock the door to opportunity."

title: Talbot Board of Ed bids farewell to 3 outgoing board members
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot Board of Ed bids farewell to 3 outgoing board members

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Words

 EASTON — The Talbot County Board of Education bid farewell to three of its seven board members at Wednesday's monthly meeting.Board Vice President Candace Henry and fellow board members Anna Howie and Mary Wheeler were thanked by their peers and Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi for their service on the board. Three new members will be sworn in next month.
"Your guidance and direction as board members has strengthened the bond between our community and our schools," Pepukayi said.
Board President Emily Jackson said the three outgoing members were crucial to the Board of Education's work to improve education in the county.
"That (work) is quietly often led by these three, which maybe you aren't aware of in the community. But I'm telling you tonight," Jackson said. "We are going to be cut down at the knees. We will grow back. But we are losing three incredibly important and valuable resources."
Wheeler, the outgoing District 6 representative who opted not to run for reelection, served on the board for 7.5 years. Cynthia Jurrius will assume Wheeler's seat after defeating Kerry Gunshenan in this month's election.
Board Member Amy Dodson said she will miss Wheeler's "pragmatism" and "common sense."
"I hope that I've done some good for the kids in Talbot County Public Schools. If I didn't, I know I tried," Wheeler said. " … Cynthia, the person who's taking my place, is here tonight. I so enjoy your enthusiasm. I've seen you at every meeting since you registered to run, so I'm pretty sure my seat's in good hands."
Howie, an assistant principal at Federalsburg Elementary School, will have her seat filled by Karla Wieland-Cherry following the District 5 election.
Jackson and Dodson said they appreciate Howie's educational expertise in her 1.5 years on the board.
"It has been such an honor and a blessing to see you in this role," Jackson told Howie. "When your name was thrown out there as somebody who could fill the empty (District 5) seat, I think I actually physically cheered. … It feels like you made a huge impact in your short time."
Henry's seat will be assumed by Ann O'Connor, who won the District 2 election over Henry. The outgoing vice president is the director of Salisbury University's Disability Resource Center.
Jackson said she's "so proud of the work" she accomplished alongside Henry, who has often spearheaded special education and accessibility efforts carried out by the board.
"As I step away from this role, I encourage you all to stay focused on what truly matters — every student, and I mean every student," Henry said. "Don't let individual agendas divide you or distract you from the essential work of seeing that every student is seen as valuable and worthy of our full support."
"I wish better for our community," she continued, "but now I get to just hold people accountable from another seat, and that's exactly what I plan to do."

As part of this recognition, nearly 50 students from Kent Island High School had the incredible opportunity to attend the Ravens game against the Washington Commanders and be celebrated for their contributions."The Interact Club, led by [teacher Lacey] Phelps has been doing remarkable work to support leadership development," Principal Dan Harding said, "under the guidance of Katie McGrath and in partnership with the Giving the Edge Foundation, run by Bobby Woolley and Colleen Williams. Williams shared their organization, Giving The Edge Foundation, was the winning recipient of the "Honor Rows" Program with the Baltimore Ravens, a program salutes youth groups that provide outstanding service to their communities. Honorees are selected by a panel of youth service leaders with the assistance of the Baltimore Ravens, the Governor's Office on Service and Volunteerism and M&T Bank staff. This year, The Edge nominated the Interact Club and Leadership Cohort at Kent Island High School.
The Leadership Cohort started in the spring of 2021 at Kent Island High School by the Giving The Edge Foundation, led by McGrath. The Foundation seeks grants to help support the program and is fully-funded by the Foundation, explained Williams.
Leadership Cohort allows student leaders to understand their "WHY." Over the years the program has grown from a handful of students to over 40+ students who voluntarily meet before school to talk about who they are, what drives their passion, and they even take a personality test. Last year an Interact portion in partnership with the Rotary of Kent Island was launched to encompass a service above self-component. This school year the Interact Club has over 70 students ready to serve and give back to their community.
At the game, the students were welcomed at the Honor Row tent where everyone received a t-shirt and ticket to the game, including VIP access where they were escorted down on the field for pictures and a chance to meet players during warm-ups. While on the field Giving The Edge Foundation was awarded a Governor's Citation for the State of Maryland. The Honor Row was also recognized on the jumbotron during the second quarter.

 CAMBRIDGE — Since terminating contracts with companies for alternative education programming for students, Dorchester County Public Schools does not plan to move forward with any new companies.At a Dorchester County Board of Education meeting Thursday, the board voted to not pursue contracts with any alternative education companies that reached out through a request for proposal.
During the meeting, DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said the district and board had reviewed the proposals and he recommends they not move forward with any of them due to "budgetary restraints."
"At this time, we cannot afford to pay for those programs," he said.
Thompson said the district will instead work to continue staffing its Positive Change Academy on Glasgow Street in order to provide alternative education to students.
In October, the board voted to terminate a one-year contract with an alternative education program for elementary and middle school students. Although board members did not comment on the decision to terminate the contract at the meeting, board member Chris Wheedleton said in an email that the actions the board took were in support of Thompson's recommendations to "equip" educators with the best resources to "get the best possible outcomes for our kids and our community."
"The board is working to encourage and support Dr. Thompson's plans to continuously review and refine the best approaches possible to create the best conditions for each of our students to thrive academically," Wheedleton said in the email.
Four months earlier, the board voted to terminate its more than three-year contract with an alternative education program for high schoolers that would have cost the district over $3.3 million. title: DCPS to examine oldest elementary school buildings as teachers demand change
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
DCPS to examine oldest elementary school buildings as teachers demand change

 November 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Sandy Hill Elementary School teachers filled the Dorchester County Board of Education meeting room Thursday to speak about the school's learning environment and the need for change.Karen McGowan, who has been a teacher at Sandy Hill for about 21 years, said their school is losing "excellent and dedicated" teachers. She said families are moving out of the district because they're concerned about sending their kids to Sandy Hill.
"Our school is old and falling apart," she said.
McGowan brought up plumbing issues in bathrooms, issues with the building's room temperatures and the difficulties of having to teach and learn in open concept classrooms. Other teachers brought up mold problems and critters and bugs getting into the building.
"There's organic growth in the building," Sandy Hill teacher Christy Starling said. "Just two years ago, we had to push back our availability to enter the building prior to school starting due to massive mold infestation that had to be treated within a month before school started."
As part of the consent agenda passed during the meeting, the board voted in favor of having architecture firm Hord Coplan Macht do an ed specifications and feasibility study for the district's oldest elementary schools, including Sandy Hill.
The ed specifications and feasibility study is being funded by Maryland's Interagency Commission on School Construction. The IAC is also allocating money for school capital improvement projects in the county once the study has been completed.
During a Board of Education work session in October, board members heard from the IAC on the different programs it operates and its projected budget allocations to Dorchester County.
For fiscal year 2026, the IAC estimates $2.75 million of its Capital Improvement Program will be allocated to Dorchester County, with a state cost share of 98%. The IAC'S Built To Learn Program, a temporary program created to hand out project-specific grants across the state, has $3.9 million budgeted for Dorchester County. Those funds need to be spent by 2031.
At the meeting Thursday, Assistant Superintendent of Administrative Services Michael Collins said it is important that the district moves forward with the ed specifications and feasibility study quickly because the IAC funding for it needs to be encumbered by the end of the year.
"We want to get this phase done so we can make big decisions on our old elementary schools," he said.
Collins said the ed speculations process will take six months. He said a committee will work with the community to get an idea of what the ideal Dorchester County elementary school looks like. The feasibility study, he said, will determine what makes the most sense for each of the schools included.
"The feasibility study basically looks at each school and says, is it feasible to either renovate this school, replace this school or combine this school in order to make it fit with the ed spec?" Collins said.
Once this process is complete, the district will be able to bid out capital improvement projects. Collins estimated it will take about a year to complete the studies.
At the end of the meeting, board member Talibah Chikwendu told the Sandy Hill teachers that she is sorry it will "take so long" to build a school.
"Because even though the things are in place for us to actually get a large amount of that money to get it done, the process takes a very long time," she said. "I am sorry that you will have to continue to work in those conditions while we do so."

title: Caroline Commissioners hear update on potential for new middle school
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commissioners hear update on potential for new middle school

 November 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners were given an update Tuesday morning on potential plans for a new middle school in the county.Bill Mengel, director of operations at Caroline County Public Schools, presented a revised fiscal year 2026 capital improvement plan to the commission. That improvement plan includes a priority item of year one and year two funding for a potential new middle school building.
Mengel noted that while the district was in the "talking phase" in August and September, it has "transitioned into the planning phase." This will soon include working with a consultant and eventually procuring a feasibility study, which may be complete in around six to eight months, Mengel said.
"One thing I've learned about building a new school is that it's a very serious endeavor," he said. "It takes a very long time to build one, approximately five years. But things change very, very quickly. That's really what kind of happened here, early October."
Currently, Colonel Richardson Middle School in Federalsburg and Lockerman Middle School in Denton serve as the district's two middle schools. It is unclear if the district will aim to build an entire new school, renovate, or add on. Mengel said those outcomes are largely dependent on the feasibility study's recommendation and the Board of Education's subsequent approval or denial.
The revised capital improvement plan was unanimously approved by the three commissioners Tuesday. Its top priority requests are $500,000 for HVAC work at Denton Elementary School and $5.5 million in early planning and design costs for a new or expanded middle school over the next two fiscal years.
$76 million in requested funding from the state for a new middle school build is listed next on the form. Mengel said that $76 million in requested state funding is around 89% of the total $86 million estimation for years one and two, meaning the county would be responsible for around 11% of the funding.
Maryland's Interagency Commission on School Construction, which the funding form will be submitted to, is looking at an approximate capacity of 126,000 square feet for a potential new build, according to Mengel. Mengel said the district's main point of negotiation is "How do we get more square footage?"
Cost per square foot has risen sharply year to year, the director of operations noted.
"If we get shovels in the ground in FY28 and we're able to move in for FY30 school year, that could be at or north of $490 per square foot," Mengel said. "So that's the driver."
Commission President Travis Breeding asked that the school district keep the county updated on the early planning and feasibility study results.
"Keep us in the loop on the study, because we would like to, if we're on the hook for 11% of this, we'd like to have input into, is it a renovation, addition, new location, all those discussions," Breeding said.
Mengel said he doesn't want work to begin on a large capital project if it's not set to accommodate increases in student population.
"I am aware, and so is the Board of Education, that there are some communities that are planned in and around Denton and points north (in) Caroline County," Mengel said. "We expect that there will be some students moving in impacting our populations. The last thing I want to do a build such as this, and then have it be at 100% occupancy within a couple of years."

title: Four Eleven Kitchen aims to feed minds and bellies through food access program
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Four Eleven Kitchen aims to feed minds and bellies through food access program

 November 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 757
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Amanda Kidd knows the importance of bringing the community to the table."A lot of times, we don't know how the person sitting next to us or across from us, how they could be the answer to a problem that we have," the Four Eleven Kitchen founder and executive director said in the nonprofit's licensed commercial shared kitchen.
"And if we never get that opportunity to really engage them, then we don't know," she said.
Reducing barriers to resources and opportunities is one of the reasons that Kidd and a group of others started a recurring community supper event in Cambridge in 2016. It's also one of goals of Feed The People, a local food access program through Four Eleven Kitchen.
Kidd said that through Feed The People, Four Eleven Kitchen aims to feed bellies and feed minds.
Feeding minds entails getting people into the kitchen to learn cooking skills and gather accessible recipe ideas. It entails farm-to-table education, which Four Eleven Kitchen is working on a curriculum for.
"We are developing partnerships and relationships that will allow us to create a curriculum and resources for the local community that desires to be first-generational farmers," she said.
The nonprofit is working with the City of Cambridge and Habitat for Humanity to turn two parcels at Douglas Street and Lincoln Terrace in Cambridge into an urban "learning" farm.
"The community will be able to go, and they'll be able to tend to the farm," she said. "But while they're tending to the farm, they're learning skills, and they're learning how to then go back and implement it."
These programs are aimed at targeting what Kidd called "a starvation of knowledge and education."
Omeaka Jackson, a Four Eleven Kitchen board member, pointed at the small number of grocery stores in Dorchester County.
"I think having a program where we talk about nutrition (and make) sure people have access to food and things like that, I just think that's something that's important in all communities, but definitely Dorchester," she said.
When it comes to feeding bellies, one of the group's goals is to bring back those community suppers that Kidd started with a group of people in 2016. Kidd said the suppers fell off with the pandemic, so they are starting from scratch.
The hope, Kidd said, is to revamp and relaunch the suppers in 2025. She said that she and the other community members involved had a long-term vision that she hopes she can carry out with Four Eleven Kitchen.
The suppers brought together an array of members from the community, Kidd said.
"It didn't matter if you made $5 a day or $500 a day," she said. "Everyone could come and eat."
Jackson said the suppers helped facilitate family conversations around the dinner table.
Kidd remembers hearing a single mom at one of the suppers talk about what a relief it was to be able to sit at the table with her kids and not worry about preparing the food or cleaning dishes.
"And then they got to have other conversations with adults while watching their kids eat and not being isolated," Kidd said. "And so what I saw was ... that experience was offering the sense of family and community."
In September, Four Eleven Kitchen opened its doors to their shared kitchen at the Packing House in Cambridge. Along with having the kitchen space, the nonprofit considers itself a food incubator hub. From cooking classes to tastings, the organization aims to connect with the community regarding all things food.
Jackson said she is "super proud" of Kidd for what she has accomplished.
"She has tenacity and a vision that anything is possible as long as you set your mind and heart to it," Jackson said.
There are multiple ways for people to support the nonprofit, including becoming a "Foodie Friend." In return for monetary donations, Foodie Friends will get access to a library and resource hub that Four Eleven Kitchen is developing. Proceeds from Foodie Friends go directly to the Feed The People program.
Along with that, there are corporate Foodie Friends opportunities where donations go toward the nonprofit's overall operation.
For Kidd, when it comes to the Feed The People program, it's all about addressing the dire — although sometimes invisible — issue of hunger. She said everyone deserves access to food when they're hungry without having to jump through a bunch of hoops.
"Let's normalize giving people the resources they need but meeting them where they are versus making them keep coming to a facility and then making them wait in line, wait for hours, when they're there because they're hungry in the first place," she said.

title: Gala at Kennard honors former educators
author: Staff Writer
content:
Gala at Kennard honors former educators

 November 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 855
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Queen Anne's County Commissioners have pledged $50,000 in funding for each of the next three years to Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center and Museum (KAACHC), while building upon the $140,000 they received from the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund, to support the hiring of an executive director to manage their programs and operations. The first installment of the county's pledge, a $50,000 check, was presented to Clay Washington, president of the Kennard Alumni Association Board of Directors, on Nov. 9, at the Kennard Gala Luncheon and Raffle event. The check was presented by County Commissioners Jim Moran and Chris Corchiarino."We are incredibly proud of the work the Kennard Alumni Association has done to preserve and celebrate African American heritage in Queen Anne's County," Moran said. "The Kennard Center has grown into a vital resource for our community, providing educational and cultural opportunities that truly make a difference. We are excited to continue supporting their mission and to see how this new funding will help expand their programs even further. The County Commissioners are committed to ensuring the success of the Kennard Center and look forward to partnering with them for many years to come."
The county assisted the Kennard Alumni Association in applying for and securing a $140,000 grant from the National Trust for Historic Preservation's African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund.
The former high school building served as Queen Anne's County's only all-Black segregated high school until segregation ended in 1966, and integration took place within the county with the opening of Queen Anne's County High School in 1967.
Left in disrepair, continuing to disintegrate over the years, a motion was made to have the former school building razed. Former alumni of the school began fundraising efforts to have the building restored instead. The efforts were led by Kennard Alumni Association President Clayton Washington, formerly of Grasonville. Washington was persistent, organizing and planning for over 15 years, until donations and grants were obtained to begin the literal renovation process.
With restoration completed several years ago, the building was dedicated in 2019. A number of events have been held there since, and the building is open to the public for rental for special private celebrations and uses.
The next big step is to hire the Kennard AAHMCC executive director.
Washington said, "We have information for applying for the position listed on our website, kennardheritage.com . We've already received a couple applications, and hope to begin interviewing people within the next 30-days. It's hoped we will have someone hired to begin work by January 1, 2025."
The KAACHC is one of only 30 sites nationwide to receive funding from the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund, which awarded a total of $3 million to historic sites representing Black cultural heritage. KAACHC has become a hub for African American history programs, exhibits, and community events in Queen Anne's County. With more than $140 million raised to date, the Action Fund is the largest U.S. resource dedicated to preserving African American historic places.
Since its establishment, KAACHC has played a vital role in providing educational and cultural learning opportunities, in Queen Anne's County. The center offers a variety of programs, including after-school mentoring, exercise classes, and summer camps for youth with special needs. With the hiring of a dedicated executive director, the center plans to expand its offerings to include adult literacy, STEM education, cultural arts, and more.
The Kennard Center is poised to become an even greater asset to Queen Anne's County, fostering connections within the community and preserving African American heritage for future generations.
Also, during the Nov. 9 program, Washington recognized and honored three former Kennard High School educators, Dr. Velma Kennedy Speight, Madelyn Matthews Hollis, and Alveta Smith Jones. Each had extensive careers in education, going well beyond teaching at Kennard.
Speight went on the teach several universities in Maryland, after serving as guidance counselor at Queen Anne's County High School. She was director of alumni affairs at North Carolina A & T University, where she had earned her bachelor's degree. Her service there was so profound, the university named one of the dormitories "Speight Hall".
Hollis transferred to QACHS where she taught until she retired, after teaching in the county for over 30-years. She then served on the county's Board of Education. Hollis was amazed that before segregation ended, African Americans could not try on clothes in stores when buying them, and personal mail could not be delivered to African American homes — they had to go to the post office to get their mail. She was a force in the community to see that the Kennard H.S. building was not torn down, but was restored to further serve the community.
Even as a child growing up on the Eastern Shore, Jones dreamed of becoming a teacher. She began her teaching career at Kennard in 1947, Jones also taught overseas, teaching sixth graders while living in Istanbul, Turkey. She then returned to teach in Prince George's County Maryland Public Schools until she retired in 1981. She, Speight and Hollis have been loyal friends all of their adult lives.
Washington presented all three ladies with plaques thanking them for their dedication to serving in education.

title: More than half of Talbot County students receive free and reduced lunches
author: Tom McCall
content:
More than half of Talbot County students receive free and reduced lunches

 November 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Life 
 
 944
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — More than half of students in Talbot County Public Schools receive free or reduced cost meals at school every week, according to the Maryland Department of Education.Free and reduced meals allow them to eat well at school.
"It is basically healthy for them. They get a fruit, a vegetable, a protein and they get a milk," said Michelle Garniga, assistant coordinator at the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center for the after school program. She has six children in TCPS.
The number of free and reduced meals in a school is a measure of poverty and food insecurity in a community.
The Maryland Department of Education found 58.41% of the students in Talbot County received free and reduced meals in 2022-2023, just under 13% higher than it was the school year prior.
At some county schools, this rate is even higher.
"What drives up the numbers are Easton Middle School and Easton Elementary School," said Catharine Poe of the Talbot Hunger Coalition, an organization of food banks and resources fighting food insecurity in the county. "Easton Elementary is 76% and the Middle School is 64%."
At other schools, numbers alone may not be enough to gauge the full scope of students' needs. Poe said the Easton High numbers trend lower because the kids do not want the other kids to know they need food.
Debbie Gardner, communications director for Talbot County Public Schools, said "We definitely talk about hunger. We consider feeding children to be one of our responsibilities in addition to educating them. We know the needs are greater than even what we see on paper."
FOOD INSECURITYThe increased rate of students receiving free and reduced meals mirrors a growing amount of food insecurity in Talbot County, where costs of food, housing and other necessities are outpacing salary growth.
"If you make $15 an hour (minimum wage) and work every single day for a 40 hour week, you only make $31,000. So if you have a family, that is not going to go very far. As soon as you have multiple children, it becomes impossible," Poe said. She said you need $38,000 for one person to make it in Talbot County.
Emily Moody, cofounder of CarePacks, said they started the nonprofit because "on weekends some kids were not eating until they got back to school on Monday morning. That is the nature of food insecurity — the uncertainty. Free and reduced meals are a lifeline. No question about it."
"Food insecurity is on the rise everywhere," Moody said. "What we have seen in the school system is an increase in the free and reduced meals program. People are working, but at wages that are not a livable wage and we live in an area where the cost of housing is really exorbitant. The cost for basic necessities like food and gas and utilities have increased. The place where the budget gets squeezed is with food at the grocery budget."
Katie Fox, community school program manager at Easton Elementary School, is the school based coordinator for CarePacks.
"Transportation impacts, if you don't have reliable transportation, which a lot of people in Talbot County don't have. That is a non-negotiable," Fox said.
And if you live in the far corners of Talbot County like Tilghman Island, it is hard to even get to a grocery store."
Moody said, "For people who are working full time to be able to afford housing and afford transportation and insurance and utilities. When those needs are met , then ideally there is room in your budget to be able to feed your family too."
It is not an issue of lazy for the working poor.
"It is not that people are not going to work. It is just that living is really expensive right now," Fox said.
FREE AND REDUCED MEALS HELPFamilies in need benefit from the free and reduced meals at the TCPS, which ensure students receive at least two meals a day for five days a week.
"It is not easy to give $4 every single day to four or five kids. That is like $24 a day. It would be fairer if everyone got free food. Just because you make more money, it is not fair for kids not to get the lunch," Garniga said.
Garniga said without the program she would be in debt and that over $100 a week for food would be a lot.
"It takes a lot of pressure off especially if you have a household with several kids. Being able to rely on the school system to provide breakfast and lunch every day, it is one of the biggest roles that the school plays," Poe said.
"They have figured out that it would save the average family $1,200 a child each year. It would end all this, and everybody who goes to school gets a free meal," Poe said.
Children in Talbot County are not alone in experiencing the benefits of free and reduced lunch programs.
At the state level, Gov. Wes Moore has signed a state Senate bill requiring the Maryland Department of Education to report to the General Assembly how much it will cost to provide free meals to all public school students in Maryland.
SB 579 opens with, "The Maryland General Assembly recognizes the positive impact on student's academic, physical and social and emotional health that results from ensuring students have access to breakfast and lunch programs while at school."
Figuring out how much it costs is the next step in pursuing universal expansion of free school meals, lawmakers argue.
The bill still needs to be funded, and it looks like the state budget is getting tighter. According to the latest briefing in the state's Spending Affordability Committee, there is a projected $2.7 billion budget shortfall that will confront the state legislature in January.

title: MSDE announces 2024 Maryland School Report Card
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
MSDE announces 2024 Maryland School Report Card

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 460
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — Highlighting school performances, the Maryland State Department of Education presented overviews and released state, district, and school-level results for the 2024 Maryland School Report Card Dec. 3.The Maryland School Report Card data describes school performance under the Maryland Accountability System for the 2023-2024 academic year. School ratings have increased overall compared to the 2022-23 academic year, according to Deputy State Superintendent Geoff Sanderson.
Based on 100 total possible points on academic and non-academic indicators that vary by grade span, schools earn points based on performance across the indicators, and points are combined into an overall result, he said.
All elementary, middle and high schools are held accountable for academic achievement, progress in achieving English language proficiency and school quality and student success, Sanderson said.
Two additional indicators for high schoolers are graduation rates and readiness for post secondary success, he said. Each school receives a total earned points percent, based on which the stars are awarded.
For Maryand's overall distribution, 41% of schools in the 2023-2024 school year earned a four- or five-star rating. About 83% of schools earned three stars or more, according to Sanderson.
Of the more than 1,400 public schools in the state, 91 schools earned the highest rating of five stars, among them 75 elementary schools, he said.
During the prior school year, approximately 80% of schools earned three stars or higher, and approximately 38% of schools earned four or five stars, Sanderson said.
In general, of the schools that changed star ratings, nearly twice as many increased their star rating as decreased, and no schools are decreasing two stars from prior year to current year, he said.
Breaking down result distribution by student race and ethnicity, on average, Black and Hispanic students earn fewer points on the accountability system than white peers, according to Sanderson.
On average, multilingual, economically disadvantaged, and students with disabilities groups earn less points than the "all student group" category in Maryland, he said.
The Maryland School Report Card includes disaggregated data showing the performance of each student group. MSDE is currently working toward improving its accountability system to be more sensitive to granularity growth, according to State Superintendent Cary Wright.
"It's got to be done student by student. It cannot be done by student group," she said.
Work seeks to utilize different benchmark systems for data collection and what kind of interventions are being provided, including gathering high quality instructional materials, Wright said.
"If you're administering an assessment, and you're not seeing any change in the next assessment, you don't just keep re-administering the assessment. It's what are you doing in between for those individual children," she said.
The Department of Education is in the process of revising its English language arts, math, social studies, science and health standards that will eventually be fed into the new assessment system, she said.

title: Caroline Board of Ed welcomes new members, elects president
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Board of Ed welcomes new members, elects president

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Chrissy Bartz and Stefanie Johnson were sworn in Tuesday as the newest members of the Caroline County Board of Education, while Michele Wayman was unanimously selected as the board's new president.Wayman, who has served on the board since 2021, was nominated for president by Board Member Troy Plutschak and confirmed in a 5-0 vote. She previously worked at Caroline County Public Schools in various teacher and administrative roles for a combined 36 years, retiring in 2009.
"I can promise you as president of your board, I will do the very best that I can do," Wayman said during Tuesday evening's meeting.
Bartz nominated Mark Jones to once again serve as vice president of the board alongside Weaver. All five members voted in favor.
Bartz, who was appointed in June to the Board of Education, ran unopposed in District 1. She is the director of community based programs at Choptank Community Health, overseeing the school-based health centers and serving as a provider at Greensboro Elementary.
In an interview, she said she's "excited" about the district's direction, particularly the fact that eight of nine schools are designated community schools by the state's education initiative, Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
"In a county that's rural, it is really important that we recognize that our schools really are hubs in our community and that we can bring a lot of resources to families and kids alongside of the education that they receive in those buildings," Bartz said. "It's a safe place for families."
Assuming outgoing President Richard Barton's District 2 seat is Johnson, who also ran unopposed. In an interview with the Star Democrat, Johnson said she's looking forward to the new role.
At first, she was hesitant about running, but the idea grew over time as she thought about her 11- and 14-year-old daughters, who both attend Caroline County schools. She said it's a great way to be a part of "conversations that can make change."
"When you're a parent sitting on the outside, you hear all of these things, and they may not necessarily make sense to you as a parent," Johnson said. "People get in their emotions and they run with that. But I'm that type of person that I want to know why, and I'm going to go straight to the source to figure that answer out."
Johnson is the executive director of the His Hope Ministries shelter in Denton and a board member for the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce.
"There's still parts of Caroline County that I haven't gotten to see or be connected with," Johnson said, "so I'm really excited to be able to go to different parts of the county and just see what's happening, see what schools are doing."
This report has been updated to correct the spelling of Michele Wayman's name.

title: Maintaining parental rights
author: Staff Writer
content:
Maintaining parental rights

 December 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 376
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I write in response to Ms. Lena Gill's letter of Nov. 30. In referring to the recent election, Ms. Gill states that the newly elected Talbot County school board members Ann O'Connor and Karla Wieland-Cherry are also members of Moms for Liberty. Ms. Gill describes the Moms as a "conservative national group" who advocate for "changes in curriculum and policies."First of all, both Mrs. O'Connor and Mrs. Cherry have repeatedly stated they are not members of Moms for Liberty; they merely participated in a debate sponsored by the Moms in which, to her credit, Ms. Jurrius also took part.
Secondly, Moms for Liberty is a support group for parents, teachers and citizens who are concerned with the education of the next generation. They provide resources for parents as well as information in educational trends throughout the country. While I have never attended one of their meetings, I do receive their newsletter and follow them on social media. Plus I have numerous friends who regularly attend the meetings.
Their agenda is to maintain parental rights through grades K through 12. Additionally, Superintendent Dr. Sharon Pepukayi, and even some of her staff, have attended three or four meetings. If it was so extreme why would they continue to return? Why is this continually portrayed by the Left as a terrible thing?
Thirdly, I wish Ms. Gill had been more specific when mentioning the "changes in curriculum and policies" that the Moms are advocating. Is she referring to better scores in English and mathematics, which the Moms advocate? Is she referring to less violence in the schools and classrooms, which they also advocate? Does she mean the schools' dispensing of contraceptives to children, opposed not only by the Moms but also by many parents?
As for the mention of concentration camps, in 2019 Trump was criticized by the Left for detention centers that had been built by Obama. Remember the children in cages? That happened under Obama, too. Trying to conflate Trump with the Nazis by mentioning "concentration camps" is actually a horrific insult to the millions of victims of the real Nazis. Plus everyone was trying to escape from Hitler's Germany. If America was so bad under Trump, why did people still risk their lives and fortunes to live here?
MARY-EILEEN RUSSELL
Claiborne

title: DCPS 'encouraged' by 2024 Maryland School Report Card
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.ccom
content:
DCPS 'encouraged' by 2024 Maryland School Report Card

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.ccom | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County Public Schools leaders pursue their goal of improving the district's state ranking in academic achievement, they are considering the recently published 2024 Maryland School Report Card results as "encouraging."According to a news release from the district, North Dorchester Middle School and Mace's Lane Middle School both gained a star on their report cards. Stars are gained using multiple indicators, including academic achievement, academic progress, graduation rate and school quality.
According to the report card, the academic achievement indicator went up 0.2 points — from 7.6 to 7.8 — overall at Dorchester elementary schools. At Dorchester middle schools, the academic achievement indicator went up 0.6 points, from 6.7 to 7.3 points. Elementary and middle schools can receive up to 20 points for academic achievement.
Dorchester high schools increased their academic achievement overall by 1.1 point, from 12 to 13.1 points. High schools can receive up to 30 points for academic achievement.
The school district news release also stated districtwide improvement in English language arts and math proficiency as well as improved graduation and attendance rates.
"While our schools have shown movement in a positive direction, some areas and schools have seen significant gains with others advancing more slowly," Superintendent Jymil Thompson said in the news release. "To achieve our ambitious goal of moving from 23rd to 15th in academic performance statewide, a larger percentage of growth is necessary. Continued focus on targeted strategies and interventions will be crucial to accelerate this progress."
Since becoming superintendent in June, Thompson has made known his hope of bringing the district's ranking up from 23rd to 15th in the state in four years. This year, the district is focusing on instructional leadership, taking a top-down approach in an effort to improve student success.
In September, Thompson told the Star Democrat that in order to jump from 23rd in the state to 15th in four years, the district will need to be consistent with developing instructional leadership and following through on it.
"Making sure that I'm having meetings with the principals, having conversations on how they're progressing on their goals," he said in September. "And if they're not progressing, how can we shift and go in a little different direction to ensure that they're meeting their goals?"
