title: Maryland State of Reading Report: 'time for a comeback after a decade of decline'
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Maryland State of Reading Report: 'time for a comeback after a decade of decline'

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — Maryland's schools are showing signs of progress in reading achievement, but a new report underscores that a deep and lasting crisis remains.The Maryland READS "State of Reading in Maryland 2025: It's Time for a Comeback After a Decade of Decline" report reveals that although incremental gains have been made among fourth-grade students, 67% still cannot read at a proficient level — a figure that mirrors the stagnation seen in eighth grade.
"We are still facing a reading crisis," said Trish Brennan-Gac, executive director of Maryland READS. "Our state is dealing with a budget crisis, including unexpected federal education cuts. Equally concerning, our report shows far too many students are not able to read proficiently."
Brennan-Gac's remarks come as state and local leaders attempt to reverse a long-term decline in literacy.
Maryland READS is a nonprofit working to improve reading instruction in the state. The organization partners with government officials and community leaders to create better policies based on research it conducts.
The report, released amid a backdrop of rising education spending — up 37% to nearly $18,900 per pupil since 2013 — provides a snapshot of Maryland's progress compared with national trends. While the state has nudged ahead of some peers in its national ranking for fourth grade reading scores, nearly two thirds of children continue to struggle.
"Reading is an investment," Brennan-Gac said. "Results will not come to fruition unless everyone works together."
The executive director stressed strong reading skills are critical not only for academic success, but for long-term outcomes like career readiness and reducing chronic absenteeism. "If a child can't read, they feel stupid and don't want to come to school," Brennan-Gac said.
Based on data provided by Maryland READS using the Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program reading scores to assess the health of reading instruction in individual districts, Mid-Shore learners fall below 50% proficiency in English Language Arts with the exception of students in Queen Anne's County.
The 2024 ELA Proficiency rates are:
Caroline: 45.5%.
Dorchester: 33.7%.
Kent: 41.2%.
Queen Anne's: 58.5%
Talbot: 47.3%.
State leaders have taken steps toward a solution by prioritizing teacher training and the development of literacy coaching programs. However, Brennan-Gac criticized recent legislation for "missing the mark" by not providing adequate funding for literacy coaches — a move she argues is essential for translating research-based practices into everyday classroom instruction.
In addition to bolstering teacher support, the report calls for a comprehensive, community-driven approach to literacy. It highlights a need for creating reading ecosystems that extend beyond the classroom and address factors such as excessive screen time — a growing barrier to the "deep reading" it says underpins comprehension and critical thinking.
"Over the last year, state leaders have led by taking action, but we need a comprehensive, community-driven effort," Brennan-Gac said. "My hope is the legislator will look at his data and start to ask why and, next year, have a different mindset."

title: High school graduation rate reaches seven-year high
author: Erin Sjostedt Capital News Service
content:
High school graduation rate reaches seven-year high

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Erin Sjostedt Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland's high school graduation rate climbed to 88% in 2024, reaching its highest point since 2017, according to the Maryland State Department of Education. The increase of nearly 2 percentage points over the previous year marks a significant recovery following pandemic-era declines.The 2024 data from MSDE shows significant gains among student groups that have historically faced barriers to graduation. Hispanic students saw their graduation rate rise over seven percentage points, while multilingual learners experienced a dramatic increase of over 10%.
"Last year was the largest year-over-year gain of any student group, and I think that's a testimony to targeted, sustained supports that are making the difference," said Theresa Timmons Parrott, an MSDE official focused on multilingual education. "It's a step in the right direction, but it's not the finish line."
Talbot County boasted a graduation rate of 95%, seven points above the state average.
Caroline and Dorchester counties both fell below the state average with rates of 87.5 and 84.4, respectively.
Statewide, female students continued to graduate at higher rates than male students, and white and Asian students graduated at higher rates than their Black and Hispanic peers. Students with disabilities graduated at a rate of 69%, still well below the statewide average. Economically disadvantaged students' graduation rate increased slightly from 2023, graduating at a rate of 82%.
The graduation rate report comes as Maryland begins to implement the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a landmark education reform law that aims to expand early childhood education, increase college and career readiness and close equity gaps.
Several of the strategies outlined in the Blueprint — including community school models and increased funding for English language learners — align with areas of progress highlighted in the 2024 data.
"If you dig down into the Blueprint, it really lays the foundation for the strategies we're seeing pay off," Parrott said. She attributes a large portion of the progress made to broaden access to early childhood education, target funding for multilingual learners, and mandate college and career readiness pathways by tenth grade.
While the Blueprint for Maryland's Future has driven recent graduation gains, lawmakers enacted adjustments this year due to a projected $3 billion budget shortfall. The Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act, passed in April 2025, includes a three-year delay in implementing teacher collaborative time and provisions to freeze increases in funding if state revenues significantly decline.
Still, regional disparities persist. While some districts reported graduation rates above 90%, others, particularly in rural counties on the Eastern Shore and in Western Maryland, sit at 80% and below. Education advocates say these gaps underscore the need for continued investment and monitoring.
"This is great news for Maryland," State Superintendent of Schools Carey Wright said in a press release from MSDE. "When we set high standards, deliver strong instruction, and invest in proven supports, our students show that they will exceed expectations."
As the 2025 graduating class enters its final year, educators and policymakers are cautiously optimistic. The latest data suggests that Maryland's post-pandemic recovery is underway, however state education officials say it will require long-term commitment to equity, funding and student support services to maintain.

title: College built as an economic engine for Shore
author: CLIFFORD P. COPPERSMITH
content:
College built as an economic engine for Shore

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CLIFFORD P. COPPERSMITH | Section: Columns 
 
 823
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Nearly 60 years after its inception, Chesapeake College remains at the center of regional progress and innovation. The college's role and mission were highlighted earlier this month when Maryland's top leaders gathered in our Health Professions and Athletics Center.Gov. Wes Moore held his cabinet meeting on our Wye Mills campus, part of an initiative to travel to every corner of the state. After that meeting, Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller and Secretary of the Maryland Higher Education Commission Sanjay Rai toured Chesapeake's skilled trades labs and new mobile welding trailer, to learn about the college's response to local economic and workforce needs and to meet some of our students.
In bringing his cabinet to our campus, Gov. Moore reinforced the college's role as a regional hub, fueling progress for the Shore. We discussed our shared priorities, like connecting Marylanders to jobs, ensuring student success and creating an equitable and robust economy.
Open-access institutions and workforce champions like Chesapeake are helping to give Marylanders a hand up to better lives — and that has always been what we're about. Conceived during the Truman Commission, the concept of the community college is part of the American Dream. As individuals set their own goals and choose their own paths to success, community colleges provide the guidance and knowledge for achieving success.
During a time of rapid change in the 1960s, Eastern Shore leaders joined together to found the college, creating a lasting resource available to all residents of our region. With foresight and a commitment to working together, the founders of Chesapeake created an institution designed to respond to the full spectrum of human interest and ability and to offer something to everyone, from transfer-bound college students to industry professional seeking new certifications to retirees enriching their lives.
Though milestones such as the Wye Mills groundbreaking and opening of the first buildings on campus in 1967 and the first commencement in 1969 would follow, the charter date of December 1965 marks the official beginning of Chesapeake College.
Remarkably, Chesapeake is still the only community college in Maryland with five support counties — a geographical area comprising nearly one fifth of the state's landmass. We're grateful for the support we enjoy from our diverse and beautiful counties, our many and varied business partners and the whole of our service community. That support has enabled this institution to endure for 60 years, in turn supporting Eastern Shore residents in finding meaningful education and employment in a wide variety of political, economic and social changes.
Even now that community-building and economy-building role continues at Chesapeake, through partnerships with county leaders, local school systems, generous donors, friends and more. In the past five years, I am proud to say that our faculty and staff have supported students to higher graduation and transfer rates; we recently ranked second in the state among community colleges, based on a study conducted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Virginia.
Looking forward, we have ambitious plans to develop cutting-edge workforce training facilities, to demonstrate that trades jobs are the "new tech" jobs and help keep Eastern Shore talent right here at home on this beautiful peninsula — not just the "land of pleasant living" but a landscape where we see abundant personal and professional opportunities.
Everyone here at Chesapeake is proud to serve our students and region, believing we are one of the most important resources to residents of the Mid-Shore and watching generations of our graduates serving their communities and giving back every day.
Acquiring skills and achieving academic success are key components of a college experience, but personal growth can contribute just as much to a student's life.
Our students develop critical thinking skills and learn how to make intellectual and interpersonal connections. Students get to know and collaborate with classmates of different ages, backgrounds and experiences. They consider the biggest challenges facing society today, and they learn to find common ground and work toward a greater good.
These experiences can't be assessed with test scores, grades or certifications. They are, however, critical for people who are able to adapt and thrive in a rapidly changing world.
I can't predict what the next 60 years will bring for higher education. The world will change in ways that we can only imagine now. Chesapeake College, as always, will adapt to those changes and continue to prepare our students for what's next in their lives as we contribute to the vitality of our community.
I hope you will help us celebrate the 60th birthday of Chesapeake College. We're planning a variety of events on campus to mark this special occasion, and you can learn more about our plans at chesapeake.edu. First up is the dedication of our new mobile welding lab on April 24 at 1:30 pm on our Wye Mills campus. If you can't visit us then, look for our mobile lab in the service area as we take our skilled trades training into the community, striving as always to meet our students wherever they are.

title: Tilghman Island celebrates opening of Judy Center
author: Konner Metz
content:
Tilghman Island celebrates opening of Judy Center

 April 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 389
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TILGHMAN ISLAND — The Tilghman Elementary School Judy Center, which opened in January, is already serving 40 families.Lori Julian, the center's coordinator, says the early learning hub is important to ensure young children and families become comfortable in a school environment.
"It's really a great transition tool to get children ready and families ready for school," Julian said.
Julian joined community members, school and center staff and state partners Wednesday to cut the ribbon on the Tilghman Island Judy Center. It's Talbot County's third center, following locations in Easton and St. Michaels.
Judy Centers are funded by the state and are a focus of The Blueprint, Maryland's expansive initiative to fund education. Last October, the state awarded a grant to Tilghman Elementary School to create one.
The centers provide workshops, family support services, enrichment and learning activities, and more for children up to five years old, according to the Maryland Department of Education. They provide most services for free for families in the school district where a center is located.
"Learning begins long before a child enters the classroom," Talbot County Public Schools Judy Center Supervisor Amy Walstrum said Wednesday. "It starts at birth."
"The earliest years are the most critical years, and the most influential people during those years are the child's first and most important teachers, who are their families," Walstrum added.
Julian has 25 years of experience as a Judy Center coordinator in Maryland, including in Queen Anne's County and recently at the St. Michaels site. The new Tilghman Island Judy Center is paramount to providing local families with resources, Julian said.
"We had (Tilghman Island) families that were coming to our St. Michaels (site), and then due to funding, we had to tell them they couldn't come anymore," Julian said. "So we lost half our families. So when we put in for this grant, we were blessed to get it here."
Julian says in a way, the Tilghman Island community has been left behind and put at a disadvantage. The elementary school only has about 100 students, community resources are limited and families have to make 20-minute drives to get to a grocery store, she said.
But the Judy Center is a significant step toward closing that gap for local families.
"Because we're such a small school, we really were surprised when we did get the grant," Julian said. "And the families were just thrilled."

title: PoliTalks transitions leadership as new era begins at Washington College
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
PoliTalks transitions leadership as new era begins at Washington College

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 822
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The founders of PoliTalks, Washington College students Stephen Hook and Zach Affeldt, are stepping down from group leadership as they graduate next month.While both are preparing for promising careers, Hook assured the crowd at their spring lecture on April 24 at Hynson Lounge that the club's future is in good hands. The event, held on the second floor of Hodson Hall, featured renowned speaker Heather Mizeur, who delivered the lecture "Disagreement is Democratic."
The lecture, free to the public, included an introduction to the new PoliTalks leadership: co-presidents Charlotte Schurman and Grace Walsh. "We feel confident in our team to take the group forward," Schurman said during a catered meal and Q&A session following Mizeur's discussion.
Schurman and Walsh are continuing the tradition of PoliTalks: to provide a safe, respectful forum for political education and conversation.
Hook reflected on the club's success during a politically charged climate, noting that he was pleased to see people with differing views engage in peaceful discussions about polarizing issues during the Trump administration.
Mizeur, a former Maryland state delegate, candidate for Congress, and CEO and founder of WeAreOne Alliance, led these discussions. This was her second time giving the lecture. She discussed the guiding principles she learned while reaching across the aisle and campaigning.
Just as she did at the Toll Science Center on Oct. 17, 2024, Mizeur introduced her mnemonic device: **RESPECTFUL**, which stands for Reciprocity, Engagement, Sovereignty, Pause, Equanimity, Curiosity, Trust, Freedom, Unhook, and Listen.
In this session, she focused on the "S" — **Sovereignty**.
Mizeur defined sovereignty as "the ability to stand in your own agency." She explained that how we respond to political disagreements, while maintaining self-control and understanding, is key to sovereignty.
Mizeur stated that the nation's collective sovereignty is currently under assault. She criticized the Trump administration for trampling due process and weaponizing fear and control, leading to the dehumanization of people.
"The initial response to these policies," Mizeur said, "is to react with fear and frustration, instead of responding with sovereignty, which is a conscious choice rooted in integrity."
Sovereignty, Mizeur explained, is a calming force that leads us to a different path, one that cannot be legislated or controlled.
"It's not earned, but inherited," Mizeur said.
She offered lessons on how to reconnect with one's own inherited sovereignty.
Mizeur emphasized that sovereignty does not mean being a doormat. It requires setting boundaries, practicing a firm "yes" and "no," and avoiding separation from others, which leads to isolation and despair. She encouraged practices like journaling, speaking with a friend or partner, and engaging in joyful activities to help individuals maintain sovereignty.
Mizeur also emphasized the importance of listening to the body's warnings and stepping back from social media to detox and nourish oneself.
"Sovereignty is a practice, not a switch you turn on and off when needed," Mizeur added.
She said practicing these principles brings deeper joy, freedom, and can spark real change in hearts and lives.
The discussion continued over a catered dinner, where guests of all ages discussed how to apply these principles in their own lives. Some shared stories of losing friends or family members over political differences and blocking people on social media. Tensions over political debates had surfaced in families.
One attendee suggested that protests, such as the "Hands Off Rally," should include what participants are fighting for, in addition to what they oppose, emphasizing the positive.
A few attendees remarked that they no longer view people with opposing views as "enemies." A central lesson from Mizeur's talk was to lead with curiosity and learn from everyone, regardless of their political affiliation.
Others acknowledged that life experiences can lead to differing viewpoints, and sometimes, religion plays a role in those differences.
One woman pointed out issues on which everyone could agree, such as the need for more jobs and affordable housing.
Hook, who founded PoliTalks after witnessing the need for peaceful discussions on campus following a Washington College lecture by conservative speaker Robert George, expressed his satisfaction with the club's success. George had cut his speech short on Sept. 7, 2023, due to protests.
"This is the best possible way we could have ended with the club," Hook said.
He thanked everyone involved, especially Mizeur, for her nonprofit work in coalition building through community partnerships. "Heather brings a unique narrative to the conversation around political dialogue that we believe is important for our community to hear," Hook said.
For those who missed Mizeur's talks, they can sign up for her newsletter and receive information about her 2025 programming at [https://www.weareonealliance.org/](https://www.weareonealliance.org/).
What's next for PoliTalks under new leadership?Schurman noted that environmental justice is a strong focus across campus. She plans to invite Serena C. McIlwain, Maryland secretary of the environment, for a future lecture.
As they call for more student involvement, PoliTalks plans to hold monthly meetings.
Several members of the Chestertown government attended the event, including Mayor David Foster and Council Member Sheila Austrian of Ward 1. Austrian found the discussion eye-opening and thanked the college and PoliTalks for reaching out to the community in such a meaningful way.

title: A dream come true: Italian exchange student spending a year in Maryland
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
A dream come true: Italian exchange student spending a year in Maryland

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 669
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Unlike Mantua, Italy, there is no opera house in Huntingtown. However, to Emma Agazzani, a resident of Italy's "Capital of Culture," living in the U.S.A. in general and Calvert County in particular has hit a high note.According to her, it's been a dream come true.
"It was something I wanted to do since I was very young," the teen told Southern Maryland News, adding that "the language, the culture, the travel" had her determined to pursue the opportunity to experience the life of a foreign exchange student.
"I applied in February 2022 with A.S.S.E.," Agazzani, 17, said.
The American Scandinavian Student Exchange has expanded since it was established in 1976. The exchange has its origins in Europe in the late-1930s. After World War II the exchange gained momentum and today over 30 countries on six continents participate.
On its website, the exchange states its mission is an effort "to foster international understanding through educational and cross cultural programs."
"My parents were hosts," Danielle Higginbotham of Huntingtown told Southern Maryland News in recalling how she and her family opened their home to Agazzani. "I knew it was something we wanted to do. We were researching students and Emma's profile stuck out with us."
Agazzani is a senior at Huntingtown High this year and will walk in the June graduation ceremony before returning to Italy later that month when her exchange program ends. She said since Italian high school is a five-year program she still has another year of secondary schooling to go in her home country before she will be off to a university.
At Huntingtown, Agazzani has been able to experience something that wouldn't be possible in Europe.
Of cheerleading, Agazzani said, "It was another of my dreams. When I think about the U.S. and high school, I think about cheerleading, because cheerleading is not a thing in Italy or Europe in general. It was my only option."
In addition to cheerleading, Agazzani has played lacrosse, a sport that hasn't caught on at all in Europe.
"I just finished lacrosse season and I really like it," she said, crediting her coaches for teaching her how to play the sport and excel in it.
Life for Emma Agazzani of Mantua at Huntingtown High hasn't been all cheers and sports, though. As a student, she is taking classes in Advanced Placement English — she has been taught English since first grade — A.P. Government, pre-calculus, biology, photography and theater.
As for what she will study in college, Agazzani said, "It's going to be something about science. I would like to be a neurologist."
When not in school, the Higginbothams have given Agazzani a chance to see America. She has traveled to several locations in Florida, including Disney World, where she donned a cheerleader's outfit for the annual Christmas parade.
While in Florida, Agazzani also got a chance to swim with dolphins.
"We tried to do a whole bunch of 'must-sees,'" Higginbotham said.
The hosts and exchange student have also traveled to New York City, Atlanta and Philadelphia.
Agazzani recalled one obligatory culinary experience in Philadelphia.
"I had the cheesesteak," she said. "That was amazing."
She also has been to Washington, D.C., and visited the White House during the annual Easter Egg Roll, meeting President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump.
Comparing the urbanized character of her hometown, with its art galleries and opera houses, to the bucolic, wide open expanse of Huntingtown, Agazzani said, "it's very different. In Italy everything is tiny and compressed. Here, everything is spread out and very big."
Of her hometown she said, "We are walkable. We have a lot of history and arts."
Agazzani summed up her Hurricane high school experience, saying, "I really like the school and this town. I'm a senior here. I think it's more interesting."
Higginbotham conceded that the experience of having a teenage cheerleader in her home has been so incredible that, while she will offer aid and advice to other families who want to participate in hosting an exchange student, for now she feels fulfillment from her experiences with Agazzani.
"She's my daughter now," Higginbotham said. "We've created a friendship, a bond."

title: Talbot council mulling $1.1 million request from school district
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council mulling $1.1 million request from school district

 May 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 706
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With less than two weeks until the Talbot County Council adopts its budget ordinance for next fiscal year, education funding hangs in the balance.Talbot County Public Schools is seeking $1.1 million in additional funds for fiscal year 2026 — $600,000 to fill nine new positions and $500,000 for teacher and staff salary increases. The former would add to the district's multilingual and special education staff, while the latter aims to inch the district closer to state-mandated $60,000 teacher salary minimums by fiscal year 2027.
District leaders say it's a "scaled-back" request from its $5.7 million ask of the county earlier this budget cycle.
"We recognize the financial pressures you face," Board of Education President Emily Jackson said at a May 6 budget hearing. "This ask is lean, deliberate and rooted in what's most necessary to keep moving forward."
In the county's budget already is $55 million for TCPS as required by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's overarching education improvement framework.
Council members are left to mull the best option as they prepare to vote on final amendments to the county's draft $161 million budget. So far, there's no clear decision.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher supported fulfilling the district's full $5.7 million request last month and maintained that stance for the pared down ask at a budget deliberation Tuesday.
"We're going to have to do it sooner or later," Lesher said. "I think it makes sense to do it this year and reduce the pain next year."
President Chuck Callahan said he feels comfortable with honoring the $600,000 part of the request to cover the new positions.
Council members Keasha Haythe, Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp have all indicated they need more time to consider options.
Any additional funding granted would result in an education supplement to the property tax rate, which is 79 cents per $100 of assessed value.
Talbot County is already mandated by the state to pay $440,000 for teachers' pensions, which will be collected through a supplement of less than half a cent per $100 of assessed value.
Three potential scenarios for tax supplements have been laid out by county staff:
Teachers' pensions only: 0.0045 per $100 of assessed value.
Teachers' pensions and $500,000 for salary increases: 0.0096 per $100 of assessed value.
Teachers' pensions and $600,000 for new positions: 0.0106 per $100 of assessed value.
Haythe said Tuesday she's trying to balance helping the school system with preventing tax increases for residents on fixed income, such as seniors.
"I am in no way, shape or form trying to discount the great work that the school system does and what the teachers do in the classroom," Haythe said.
At last week's hearing, teachers and parents advocated for the council to include the $1.1 million. Lisa Hayes, a parent of three TCPS graduates, said past education investments are paying off now as her children enter the workforce.
"You cannot not fund a budget for our children's education because there is nothing more important than that," Hayes said.
Andy Burke, president of the Talbot County Education Association, which functions as the teachers' union, made his case.
"We continue to see too many educators migrate away to the higher wages and salaries paid in neighboring public school systems," Burke said.
In an emailed statement, TCPS Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones said the district made "very difficult choices" to reduce its request to the county.
Jones noted staff will present the Board of Education with a budget amendment package in June, which will adjust the $86 million unrestricted budget the board OK'd in February.
"We will eliminate most of the new positions we had requested," Jones wrote. "We will scale back our requests and defer programs that will have the least direct impact on our goals for our students."
A final decision by the county on the $1.1 million in question, as well as the entire FY26 budget, is expected at the council's May 27 meeting.
While no clear choice was made during Tuesday's deliberations, county and district leaders did agree that state mandates and formulas are creating the tricky fiscal situation.
"It's just become screamingly clear that there's a disconnect at the state level between the requirements that they're putting on local schools across the state, and the funding formulas that are articulated to county governments to pay for their education," said County Manager Clay Stamp.

title: 100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin
author: Konner Metz
content:
100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin

 May 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 664
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over the last 100 years, the Talbot County Free Library has adapted to societal changes such as the creation of the Internet, economic downturns like the Great Depression and, most recently, a global pandemic.As the world changes around it, the organization's staff and volunteers are ensuring sure the library keeps up. Executive Director Dana Newman believes the library is well-positioned to serve the community's needs for years to come.
"I do think the library will continue to move with the future, and it will continue to be here," Newman said.
Serving residents across the entire county, the Talbot County Free Library has oriented itself as a hub for the county. Between a physical collection of over 130,000 books and other items, computer and technology access, and hundreds of free programs, Newman says the library has more resources available than most people would think.
This October, the library will host a centennial gala, an opportunity for many to celebrate the library's history and its impact on residents in the 100 years since its inception.
Emma Poole, TCFL's communications manager, was born in Easton and still has her original library card from when she was 3.
"This has always been such a safe space for me," Poole said. "My parents brought me here all the time. I begged my mom to bring me to the library. I'd drag her out of the house."
During college, Poole used the library's expansive Maryland Room collection in writing her historical thesis. And now as a staff member, Poole recognizes the institution's purpose in Talbot County extends far past books and research.
"It's so much more than books," she said.
ADAPTING OVER TIME
On Oct. 15, 1925, Talbot County Free Library opened in two rooms in the Tred Avon Building on South Washington Street. Caroline Burnite Walker founded the library, which began with an 800-book collection.
She was a longtime children's librarian, and the early days of Talbot's library focused on serving the youth. Scotti Oliver, current assistant director, says the organization's "emphasis has always been on children's services."
The library offers many early literacy programs, partners with local schools and will host the 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival this June.
TCFL moved inside the courthouse in the 1940s and soon became one of Maryland's first county-wide public library systems. Around three decades later, it moved to West Dover Street, where it sits today.
Ever since its founding, the nonprofit has constantly adapted, library leaders say.
"I think we demonstrated over time that when people think, 'Well maybe the library's a thing of the past,' it's not," Newman said. "Because there's a new need, and there's a need for instruction. We are a learning institution."
Among the many offerings are book clubs, community meeting rooms, a free collection of seeds, tax assistance aid and social services programs.
Following the pandemic, Newman says the organization reinvented itself in a way, focusing much more on digital literacy classes, availability of computers and devices, and internet access.
Newman noted the library has demonstrated an ability to pivot when needed, a skill that'll help tackle future challenges — one being the rise of AI.
COMMUNITY LINCHPIN
While the library's main branch is in well-populated Easton, TCFL is undergoing renovations to its branch site in St. Michaels. The building will expand and add children's spaces.
One of Newman's hopes is that the Bookmobile service can return. Ending in the 1990s due to a lack of funding, the Bookmobile made trips to remote parts of the county such as Tilghman Island, Cordova and Trappe. Newman said the library understands the importance of reaching these communities, and is looking to secure funding for the venture in the near future.
Around 20,000 county residents hold a library card, over 7,000 of them children. Like Poole, many of those cardholders consider the library a safe place. Newman emphasized that unhoused individuals often rely on that "safe space."
"Libraries exist because people have a need, and we're serving that need as much as we can," Newman says. "And that need continues and has continued for many, many years."

title: Robbins YMCA opening reading hub to tackle childhood illiteracy
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Robbins YMCA opening reading hub to tackle childhood illiteracy

 May 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 500

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Robbins YMCA is stepping up after Dorchester County Public Schools faced significant budget cuts this year.The school district started this budget season with a $10 million deficit. Addressing that deficit meant Dorchester County schools lost after-school and summer programming.
The cuts to education come at a time when the county ranks 21st out of 24 school districts (including Baltimore City) in third grade literacy and 22nd out of 24 in overall English Language Arts proficiency in the state.
The Y is partnering with the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation to create a space for the Dorchester County Campaign for Grade Level Reading, a campaign that aims to target childhood illiteracy.
{span}The campaign was inspired by the movie "Sentenced," which was produced and narrated by NBA champion Stephen Curry. The film explores the epidemic of childhood illiteracy and its lifelong impacts.{/span}
"Dorchester County has, for a long time, been ranked very low in the state of Maryland," said Matthew Peterson, executive director of the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation. "And so interestingly, now concurrent to all the work that the Y is doing, that we're all doing together, Dorchester County Public Schools is undergoing a strategic plan to go from 21st, to 15."
The Dorchester County Campaign for Grade Level Reading plans to approach this goal from multiple angles and with multiple partnerships.
Because third grade is a pivotal marker for childhood learning development, the campaign's target population are children from birth to age 5, so they are better prepared to enter kindergarten, and are less likely to fall behind.
"So we're trying to grab moms as prenatal because we're gonna do infant groups, we're gonna do, you know, toddler groups, mommy and me groups, so we want to bring awareness at early childhood," said Tynice DeShields, director of mental health at the YMCA of Chesapeake.
The campaign's partners include county schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson, the Dorchester County Public Library, United Way of the Lower Eastern Shore, Operation Pathways and volunteers from the community.
"There's a number of agencies we've been working with over the years. You know, as any organization, some were more engaged than others, and so bringing everybody on board, finding out where that alignment fits best, and then trying to leverage that, to do the best we can, is what we've always tried to have," Peterson said.
The reading hub will be a space that is open to the public and YMCA members alike.
"We're building this reading hub as a meeting place where we can have a resource center, we can have meetings with the community, we can have sessions with the parents to teach their kids how to read, how to look at letters and numbers, and not just throw a book in front of them," said Bryant Wittington, director of the Dorchester County Campaign for Grade Level Reading.
Peterson, DeShields and Wittington are excited to engage with the community and hope to build a strong foundation of volunteers at the reading hub.
"We want to build that unity in the community," Wittington said.

title: It's time to pause state's education blueprint
author: DAVID REEL
content:
It's time to pause state's education blueprint

 May 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 762
 Words 

 Read News Document

 One of the issues in Maryland's state government and political arena that has generated recurring and intense debate, is funding for a 10-year educational improvement initiative known as the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, also referred to as the Blueprint or as Kirwan.The goals for Kirwan include expanding participation in pre-kindergarten programs, more funding for schools with high concentrations of poverty, increasing pay and opportunities for teachers, and creating career pathways for high school students.
With regard to pre-kindergarten, the Kirwan plan has two specific and measurable goals.
First, in 10 years, 80% of all 4-year-olds and all 3-year-olds are to be enrolled in pre-kindergarten programs, up from 40% in the 2023 school year.
Second, achieve the first goal by using a "mixed delivery system" using public school pre-kindergarten programs and private pre-kindergarten providers.
To date, achieving those goals has been elusive and may not occur on the current schedule.
A headline in one recent Maryland media outlet article was, "Even as spending rises, under half of Maryland 4-year-olds attend public pre-K."
The article references reports from the National Institute for Early Education Research at Rutgers University. They note that Maryland lags behind 17 other states enrolling kids in public pre-kindergarten programs, despite spending thousands more per child than it used to.
Last school year, 38% percent of 4-year-olds in Maryland were enrolled in state-funded pre-K programs, down one spot in the national rankings from the previous year.
Last year, 7% of 3-year-olds in Maryland were enrolled, also one spot below the previous year.
Rutgers reports those results occurred despite Maryland spending $358 million in state funds and an additional $3.8 million in federal pandemic recovery funds.
How much Maryland spent per pre-kindergartner, including federal recovery funds, is up $3,979 from the previous year.
With regard to the goal expecting greater involvement from private prekindergarten providers in an expanded pre-K program, current participation to date, is lower than expected.
In a survey of the state's private childcare providers, only 12.9% of respondents said they plan to or were already involved in the pre-K program created under the Blueprint.
More than a third of the 256 respondents said they were unsure whether they will participate in the pre-K expansion and nearly 40% said they would not. 12.9% of the survey responders had never even heard of it, the same as the percentage of those who are already involved in it.
All this news is in addition to sobering reports from the General Assembly's nonpartisan legislative budget analysts.
They are projecting that by next year, the state's structural budget deficit will grow to $1 billion. In fiscal 2027, the last year of Governor Moore's first term, it grows to $1.3 billion. A year later, it more than doubles to $3 billion.
That certainly helps explain Moody's downgrading the state's fiscal outlook from stable to "negative," citing looming structural deficits driven by state funding needed for Kirwan.
In its report, Moody's wrote, "The negative outlook incorporates difficulties Maryland will face to achieve balanced financial operations in coming years without sacrificing service delivery goals or adding to the weight of the state government's burden on individual and corporate taxpayers."
This news means the leadership of the General Assembly and Gov. Moore need to engage further in bi partisan dialogue and deliberations on tough decisions regarding revisions to Kirwan.
That is not unprecedented.
Gov. Moore and the General Assembly leadership did that prior to the end of the 2025 General Assembly session. There was bipartisan agreement on and support to delay a Kirwan mandate for local school districts to increase teacher collaborative time for curriculum planning, grading and professional development outside of the classroom.
About that outcome Moore said, "Two years before I was sworn in as governor, the General Assembly passed a historic piece of education reform. But, like any big law of ambition and bold aspiration, we knew that there would have to be responsible adjustments and enhancements that had to be made."
The revisions made on teacher collaborative time were a good step but is not nearly enough.
The governor must call for a special legislative session as soon as possible this year and well before the next regular 90-day session that convenes in January 2026.
He must also ensure the sole focus for that special session is next steps for Kirwan.
The best outcome of that special session should be twofold.
Bipartisan approval to a pause on all state funding for Kirwan until a date certain in the future.
Bipartisan approval of a pause on all new mandates for local school boards, until a date certain in the future. They know best about student needs and limits on funds to meet those needs.
Maryland citizens and Maryland taxpayers deserve nothing less.

title: Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALESTOWN — After former North Dorchester High School baseball coach Dan Hortert's home was severely damaged by an EF-1 tornado, the community rallied around him to help pick up the pieces.Members of the baseball and softball teams, teachers, parents and former students responded to a Facebook post encouraging them to come out and help. The response was overwhelming.
People showed up with tractors, cranes, homemade cookies, pizza and determination to Hortert's Galestown, Delaware home Saturday morning.
"It's just unbelievable," the coach said through tears as he looked around at the support. "The Dorchester community as a whole is a whole lot closer than people can even describe," he said.
Hortert officially retired from North Dorchester High School last year. He was a beloved science teacher and baseball coach.
He has lived with his wife Kathy in their Galestown home for the past 50 years, and their daughter Angela lives in the home next door.
The damage to Hortert's home was mainly caused by two trees in the front yard. One of the trees snapped at the base, breaking through the house's roof, and the other was completely uprooted, destroying a shed in the backyard.
The family and one of their cats were in Hortert's home during the tornado, sheltering under the staircase. They got through the storm unharmed.
The cat had delivered a litter of kittens a few weeks prior, and the young cats were living in the garage. As soon as the tornado passed, Angela ran out to check on them, and they were also unscathed. "It all happened so fast," she said.
Hortert said the day after the tornado hit, community members began coming by asking how they could help.
"You know, Hortert's a great guy. He'll probably do anything for anyone. He's very willing to help, especially the youth," said North Dorchester High School senior TJ Leonard. This sentiment was echoed by several of the other volunteers gathered Saturday morning.
Hortert said that 50 years of teaching showed him how good the kids are at heart.
"The public schools are getting a bad rap, and North Dorchester in particular gets that from time to time, but its a wonderful school with wonderful kids that are a wonderful community," Hortert said.

title: Easton, St. Michaels high schools celebrate graduates
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton, St. Michaels high schools celebrate graduates

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 523
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Seniors at Easton High School and St. Michaels High School marked the end of a four-year chapter with graduation this week, celebrating accomplishments and looking forward to the future.On Wednesday, 291 graduated from Easton High. Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi said during her address to the class that the school's yearbook showed just how close students and faculty were during the last four years.
"What stood out the most were the connections I saw," Pepukayi said. "As I turned each page, I saw smiles, I saw groups of students clustered together. … I saw laughing, talking, joking taking place between the students, among students, in between staff and students."
Pepukayi emphasized to the graduates that creating those human connections is vital, especially in a world influenced by artificial intelligence.
"I read that Generation Z, who are the ages of 18 to 28, require a higher level of human connection, whether it's at home, at school, or in places of business," Pepukayi said. "Human connection. Now in the AI-driven world, this is of utmost importance. And that human connection is very evident in this class."
Easton High valedictorian Mia Mazzeo shared a similar theme in her speech.
"When all the information in the world is just a click away, take that extra step and dig deeper," Mazzeo said. "An eagerness to learn and an attentive teacher is all one really needs. It is only when you question how the world works that you can truly change it."
Mazzeo told her classmates that wisdom comes from interactions with one another.
"When I look back at my time in high school, I think I grew the most during late-night conversations with friends and after school chats with teachers," she said. "The experiences you share with others and the advice they have to offer is priceless."
ST. MICHAELS HIGH
On Thursday, 60 seniors at St. Michaels High School threw their caps in the air and joyously celebrated the achievement of being a newly-minted graduate.
Valedictorian Alexandria Rockwell said the Class of 2025 showed "incredible purpose" and encouraged her classmates to maintain that same drive as they go their separate ways.
Rockwell said the last four years tested and pushed the graduating class.
"As we entered high school, many challenges were thrown at us," she said. "Four years felt like forever. But now we're here. It's gone by in a flash, and it's bittersweet because we looked forward to this moment for so long, but now we know we're leaving behind something we'll never quite return to."
School principal Theresa Vener echoed that Thursday's graduation was bittersweet, bidding farewell to the graduating class she's been alongside since starting as St. Michaels Middle High School principal seven years ago.
Vener, retiring this year after 32 years working for the district, was presented with an honorary diploma at Thursday's ceremonies. Students, staff and district administrators thanked her for her dedication and leadership.
The outgoing principal said it was an "absolute privilege" to watch the Class of 2025 grow into caring and confident young adults.
"I have watched you fall, get back up and take those steps forward," Vener said. "One step at a time, but 'always forward,' just like your class motto says."

title: A day for children at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A day for children at the library

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 821
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When I was 3 years old, my parents told me there would soon be a new addition to our family, that my mother was going to have a baby.At that age, my two favorite things in the world were TV cowboys and Coca-Cola, which inspired me to come up with the perfect name for my new brother or sister. I began to declare confidently (and often) that we should name the child "Coco Bang-bang."
When my parents finally admitted they were thinking along different lines, maybe "Catherine" or "Robert," I began to have serious doubts about the whole enterprise.
For my entire life (which, at 3, stretched back toward infinity), I had been the center of Mom and Dad's world; the idea that I might now have to share their affections with some poorly named interloper rubbed me the wrong way.
I think my parents must have suspected my misgivings because about a month before the blessed event was to occur, they gave me a new picture book. I no longer remember the title of that tiny tome, but I do remember what it was about: a little boy, who looked a lot like me, was excited about the new baby his parents were about to bring home.
Actually, what I remember best about the book is a single illustration.
As I recall, it shows a scene that takes place immediately after the new addition to the family has arrived home from the hospital. The little boy sits on a couch. His parents have placed a pillow on his lap, and upon the pillow they have laid the child, its tiny hands lifted wonderingly toward the little boy's smiling face.
Immediately, the idea that I too might sit on our couch, a pillow on my lap, an infant lying upon it, took possession of my impressionable 3-year-old mind. And, as I recall, my parents wisely allowed me to realize that fantasy when my little sister Cathy finally did come home from the hospital.
I could be wrong, but it's my guess that picture book — whatever its title — probably saved my sister from a fair amount of brotherly pestering.
Which leads me, naturally enough, to the benefits accruing to children from books. On Saturday, June 7, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., come rain or shine, the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library will host the 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival.
This year's festival will feature 22 children's book authors and illustrators, all of whom underwent a rigorous vetting process before being selected to participate.
Children who sign up at the festival for the library's Summer Reading Program will receive a free cookie (while supplies last) imprinted with the festival's crab logo, courtesy of All in the Mix Bakeshop, and a voucher good for one free book (once again, while supplies last) from the attending author of their choice. It's always fun to see the pride children take in asking the author they've selected to sign the book they've received.
This year's festival will offer children some great books to choose from. Here's a small sampling of the many works that will be on display:
Danielle Joseph's young adult novel "Shrinking Violet" was adapted into the Disney Channel movie "Radio Rebel."
Colleen Kosinski's "A Home Again" is so popular, it's been translated into seven languages.
Trinka Hakes Noble's "The Day Jimmy's Boa Ate the Wash," (ALA Notable, PBS Reading Rainbow feature, American Book Award) has just celebrated its 45th year in print.
Jennifer O'Connell's beautifully illustrated picture books include "The Eye of the Whale," winner of the Green Earth Book Award, and The New York Times bestseller "Ten Timid Ghosts," which has sold more than a million copies.
And Timothy Young (who first conceived of the Chesapeake Children's Book Festival) has set his middle-grade chapter book "Mac and the Millstone of Time" at the Old Wye Mill in Wye Mills.
Traditionally, the festival resembles a small, library-sized carnival, designed to create a special day of fun for little ones. The Maryland State Opera Bears will be back for a return engagement this year, the Daughters of the American Revolution will offer crafts, the Judy Center will have their Make-A-Book table, the Master Gardeners will assure that Mother Nature provides an important part of the day's excitement, and Raising a Reader will set up a story walk.
Maryland Public Television, The Imagination Library, Radcliffe Creek School and Friends of the Library will also be on hand to keep the day entertaining.
The Friends of the Library are the primary sponsors of both the Festival and the Summer Reading Program. Other festival sponsors this year include Maryland Public Television, Easton Utilities, Talbot County Government, Talbot Arts and the Maryland State Arts Council.
All in all, the Talbot County Free Library's 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival should be a special day for children. And those parents out there thinking about bringing a new baby into the world can rejoice. The name "Coco Bang-bang" remains available for their consideration.

title: 'Green School' programs in Caroline County bring joy to students
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chesoub.com
content:
'Green School' programs in Caroline County bring joy to students

 May 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chesoub.com | Section: News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — As of this year, Two Caroline County public schools have been certified as Green Schools by the Maryland Association for Environmental and Outdoor Education.Denton Elementary joined Greensboro Elementary in gaining the certification this year. Both schools went through a two-year application process through MAEOE to be come Green School certified.
Although directors for programs at the schools said the program was intense, they said the help they received from the community was surprising and made the process go much smoother.
"You have to work together, and we divided and conquered," said Julie Strange, pre-k teacher at and program coordinator for Green Schools at Denton Elementary. "You have to contact people at the board office. You have to contact contact your cafeteria. You have to contact people I didn't even know did jobs.
"It's an intense process, but again, eye-opening how helpful everybody was and that there are people for everything."
Within that application for the program there are different subcategories for which the schools must show evidence they met the objective.
The application also comes with a curriculum that must be completed by the students, and the school must provide one example of outdoor or environmental instruction per grade level.
"Through our curriculum and standards, we're able to teach these kids sustainability practices and how to take care of the Earth, just learning about the Earth through those environmental literacy standards. It's one of my passions. I really enjoy doing it," said Zellie Kneller Kidigarden, a teacher and program director for Green Schools at Greensboro Elementary.
Throughout the application process, the elementary schools have been able to produce multiple projects that help compost, save energy and grow fresh foods.
One project at Denton Elementary involves collecting breakfast bags in the morning after breakfast. According to Strange, the school lets third graders create boxes and put recycle signs on them to put in their classrooms to collect bags in the morning.
"Every day, we get breakfast in plastic bags per child, and our school is about 650 kids. So that's 650 bags that go in the trash every day," Strange said. "The kids were so excited about it, and they did it... the kids are responsible for putting their bag in there when they're done their breakfast instead of throwing it in the trash."
One of the projects Greensboro Elementary conducts is planting in multiple gardens.
"We do strawberries, herbs in our garden tower and then we have our pollinator garden. Our Environmental Club also planted native plants everywhere in our swales. Before the end of the school year, we're going to plant native plants in our courtyard," Kneller said.
Kneller credits community partners for being helpful in their pursuit to becoming a green school.
Some of the organizations Greensboro Elementary has partnered with are Pickering Creek Audubon Center, Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Tuckahoe State Park, Wetlands on Wheels and many more.
"I'm so grateful that we're a community school because being a community school allows us to work with... stakeholders in the community, and we get wonderful things from all the members in the community," Kneller said.
Greensboro Elementary has been a green school since 2021 and will go through a renewal next year. The school has been able to secure multiple grants that will lead to future projects, including tree planting and much more.
Both Kneller and Strange believe every school should be Green School certified.
"It's really, really, really important work and every school should be green school certified," Kneller said. "It is life-changing for a lot of students and adults and I would say everyone because this is the planet that we live on and everyone needs to learn how to take care of it because we don't have anywhere else to go."

title: Lockerman Middle School Committee heard and addressed concerns at second meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Lockerman Middle School Committee heard and addressed concerns at second meeting

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 634
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Lockerman Middle School Committee meeting Monday night, Robyn Toth, architect for the new Lockerman Middle School, confirmed that after the state's assessment, the current Lockerman Middle School building cannot be renovated, and the county will go with a new building."We've already reached out to the state and said the renovation of this existing facility as a school is not feasible," Toth said at the meeting. "It is my understanding that (the current school is) going to become a community center. So, this building is going to stay. It's going to keep its history."
Though it was never indicated as a preferred option, staying at the current site and renovating was left on the table at prior committee meetings and discussions on the new school.
The May meeting featured two potential locations for a new school, the first location would be behind North Caroline High School, and the second would be on Double Hills Road in Denton.
After a public hearing at that meeting, the committee came back with models and options for the school at two potential new locations.
"There was a lot of feedback last time about the safety issue for buses coming and going, as well as parent drop off," Superintendent Derek Simmons said. "So, I think the architect did the best they could with the two existing locations that the county has told us to look at to kind of make them as usable as possible."
The presentation given Monday premiered three building layout options for the North Caroline High location and two options for the Double Hills Road location.
The North Caroline High design options included two plans for a two-story style building with wings separated by grade level. Though these designs for the building itself are identical, the building is located in different places on the lot in each design.
One option proposes relocating the North Caroline High baseball and softball fields to a different location. The other keeps the middle school on the left and everything belonging to the high school on the right side of the property.
The third design option would also involve relocating the fields and would also relocate the solar array on the site. The existing barn and fenced pasture would also be rebuilt in a new location.
This third option is a three-story building design, with each floor being a different grade level.
"The different locations on North Carolina High School was interesting," Simmons said. "I think most of us in our heads ahead of time could envision it in one spot, but giving the flexibility of the options really opened up some some pathway."
The Double Hills Road location designs featured the two- and three-story options as at the North Caroline location.
While both options propose that the solar panels currently at the site may need to be located another portion of the county property and that new pump station will need to be constructed, entrance options, building locations and parking locations are different.
"Double Hills Road with the new county road going in in that property does preserve a 20 plus acre plot for to use," Simmons said. "It's good location but again it gives us that flexibility now to see what the buses would look like coming and going. What drop off would look like, what staff parking would look like because there's nowhere near enough staff parking here as well."
Now that the Lockerman Middle School Committee has presented all options, the public will have until before June 9 to respond to an online survey with their comments.
The top ranked designs for both locations will be presented to the Caroline County Board of Education in July. Then the Board of Education will make a decision on a location no later than August to make sure the timeline for construction stays on track.
To participate in the survey, visit carolineschools.org/article/2241492.

content:
North Caroline grad celebrating more than a high school diploma

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 DENTON — Sa'Mauria Ennals graduated from North Caroline High School last month, but she celebrated way more than a high school diploma.Along with graduating from North Caroline, Ennals graduated from Chesapeake College with an advance transfer certificate and became a certified nursing assistant through Chesapeake College's nursing program.
Ennals maintained GPAs between 3.6 and 3.7 at both the high school and Chesapeake College. She plans to attend Towson University and major in nursing starting in the fall. She will already be multiple semesters ahead.
Ennals' love for health care came during her freshman year of high school, but she decided she wanted to be a neonatal intensive care unit nurse during her sophomore year.
"When I just like actually sat down and was able to research and just gather data on all these different branches, that's what really like sealed the deal for me," she said.
Ennals is not the first child of her mother, Maria Bowser, to participate in the dual enrollment program at Chesapeake College. Ennals' two older sisters participated in the program in Talbot County, both graduating with a plethora of college credits to pursue nursing.
Ennals knew from watching her sisters complete dual enrollment classes that the workload was difficult, but she knew she was up to the task.
Ennals said she faced challenges getting enrolled in the courses she needed.
After an auditorium presentation with all juniors at North Caroline explaining dual enrollment options, Ennals went to her guidance counselor to talk about the process of doing dual enrollment and potentially graduating from Chesapeake College before graduating from high school.
"I tried to bring it up to my guidance counselor and they kind of deterred me from taking the dual enrollment classes, and that's when we decided to have a meeting about that and that's what got me into those classes," Ennals said.
"My guidance counselor told me that it was going to be too hard for me, which I was very confused as to why they would think that because I was already ahead when I first came to that school."
Bowser and Ennals met with counselors at North Caroline for several weeks about what course work would be best for Ennals.
"If she wants to be a nurse, and she knows she's going to college, college classes are the better path for her. However, we got a little pushback," Bowser said.
A representative from Caroline County Public Schools said the district was unable to discuss conversations between students, parents and employees.
After more pushback, Bowser and Ennals began to work with the Gabrilla Moreland, TRIO Upward Bound academic coordinator, and Mark Berry, director of TRIO program at Chesapeake College.
The TRIO Upward Bound program offers high school students from Caroline, Kent and Talbot counties an opportunity to gain college and career readiness skills, through tutoring, workshops and field trips at no cost to students.
The group set down with county Board of Education and came up with a plan to allow Enalls to take four college classes during her junior year of high school.
"I wasn't taking the 'no she can't take classes because it's too hard.' How was it too hard? She had a 4.0, and she was managing everything and had all of her high-school credits by her 11th grade year," Bowser said.
Ennals said it became a "prove them wrong type of situation."
"I loved it because it was a lot of motivation knowing that there were education officials telling me that I can't do something. So I just used that as motivation to just let me get through it. Let me kind of not only prove to myself but also prove to them," Ennals said.

title: MidShore Meals til Monday launches summer meals program for kids
author: Lily Tierney
content:
MidShore Meals til Monday launches summer meals program for kids

 June 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 322
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — On Tuesday, MidShore Meals til Monday rolled out its children's summer hunger relief program with its brand new big blue van, which was partially funded by No Kid Hungry and Preston Automotive.Founded in 2017, Meals til Monday has been a successful initiative that sends breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks home with children who may not get them otherwise.
The summer program began last year and aims to target child hunger in Dorchester County, according to MidShore Meals til Monday's website. After facing a $5.59 million deficit for fiscal year 2026, Dorchester County Board of Education made cuts to afterschool and summer programs to balance the budget, according to a report by the Star Democrat in March.
According to MidShore Meals til Monday's website, one in five children doesn't know where their next meal is coming from and goes to school without enough to eat to fuel their bodies or brains. In 2024, 95% of students in Dorchester County qualified for free or reduced-price meals, according to the Maryland State Department of Education.
The Community Eligibility Provision meal program is a meal service for schools and school districts in low income areas and allows schools to offer breakfast and lunch at no cost. According to Meals til Monday's website, approximately 5,000 students in Dorchester County participate in this program.
However, the program is not available during the summer, which is where Meals til Monday comes in.
The summer meal program offers one meal box for each child per household. Each box contains seven complete breakfasts and lunches, including an entree, fruit and vegetables. Milk is optional, and a weekly menu, reheat instructions and food safety information are also provided in each box, according to the summer meal program registration page.
Meals til Monday's summer program will run from June 23 to Aug. 21. One-time registration is required and can be done online through the DCPS website or at one of the 10 sites during pick up.

title: Ed Spec Committee recommends North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Ed Spec Committee recommends North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 467
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Board of Education is one step closer to picking a new location for Lockerman Middle School.At the monthly Board of Education meeting Tuesday, the Lockerman Middle School Ed Specs Committee said that after the feasibility study and community input, the recommended location for the new school is on the same property as North Caroline High School.
Board of Education members decided not to formally vote on a location after receiving almost two hours of information from the Ed Specs Committee. The board decided to push the decision back to the August meeting.
Multiple reasons came forward on why the North Caroline High site was recommended over the Double Hills Road site.
"Some of the highlights that came out throughout the analysis and the surveys was again, the infrastructure. If you're not spending a lot of money on that, the site readiness, the educational alignment, a lot of really exciting ideas came out during the community meeting of ways that you could really have mentorships and things like that with the older and the younger students being on one site," said Robyn Toth, architect for the new school.
Reason included the use for indoor and outdoor activities and the ability to share space for events at North Caroline High.
"There's clear paths for the indoor and outdoor activities," Toth said. "There's no crossing of streets, lots of capabilities there also because you are sharing more spaces… There were some concerns about large events and right now, if they're at Double Hills or if they're at Lockerman now, where do we go for these large events? That don't happen that often and you don't necessarily need to build more space that the state's not going to support. Well, you've got a high school right there that's got a large auditorium. It's got a large gym."
With the North Caroline High location, development prices will be about $500,000 cheaper. The site development for the North Caroline High location will be $10 million, while Double Hills Road would cost $10.5 million.
Although in the community meetings multiple builds were shown, the new middle school, regardless of the location, will be a two-story building with a two-wing design.
According to the Ed Specs Committee Powerpoint, the new anticipated project budget would be $103.82 million with state funding coming in at around $80 million and local funding covering the remainder.
The only concerns brought up about the North Caroline High site were the solar array on the property and the traffic Central Avenue could receive from a new school being added to the location.
To purchase the solar panels on the property, it would cost about $180,000, which doesn't include the cost of relocation.
The Board of Education will take all the information received and make a decision on what location will be picked at its August meeting.

title: Dorchester schools prepare for more cuts
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Dorchester schools prepare for more cuts

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 322
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Dorchester County Public Schools are projected to lose over $642,000 in federal funding after the Trump Administration suddenly announced the decision to withhold $6.8 billion in federal education cuts, according to DCPS communications specialist Casey O'Bier.The U.S. Department of Education cut 28 K-12 programs saying "states and localities, not the Federal government, are best suited to determine whether to support the activities authorized under this program or similar activities within their own budgets and without unnecessary administrative burden imposed by the Federal government," or stating the program has not been proven effective, or that cutting funding is to restore fiscal discipline in the states.
In an email to the Star Democrat, O'Bier said those cuts will impact a variety of programs including teacher training, internal and external student experiences, and English Language Learner programs.
"DCPS would need to reallocate existing funds to sustain programs that were originally funded through some of these federal grants or eliminate various programs in a worst-case scenario," O'Bier stated as one of the district's central concerns.
The federal funding cuts to education come at a time when Dorchester County Public Schools are already struggling financially.
In January, DCPS faced a budget deficit of $10.19 million, which they reduced to $5.59 million in March. To further reduce the deficit, DCPS got rid of their after school and summer programs.
The county had to reduce staff sizing, but Superintendent Jymil Thompson said he wants to keep class sizes small and retain teachers at all costs.
The Board of Education has been making concerted efforts to move DCPS from 23rd out of 24 school districts — including Baltimore City — in state education ranking, but the federal funding cuts make those efforts more difficult.
"Moving forward, we will be proactively looking closely at unique ways to reallocate pre-existing funds to support the inclusion of these federally funded programs which are a major asset to Dorchester County Public Schools and the enrichment of its students," O'Bier said.
